[h2]Gameplay & Mechanics[/h2]
Portal 2 (2011) retains its unique puzzle solving mechanics from Portal (2007), where the player has control of a “Portal Gun”, a device which allows the player to shoot 2 “portals” on any applicable surface which connect those two places into one, similar to teleportation. The player can see through these portals to what’s on the other side, and momentum is carried through the portals which create some interesting opportunities for speeding through the air, shooting portals as you go, reaching the exit of a level without even having to touch the ground (which at times makes the game feel more like a speedrunning platformer, it’s a brilliant combination). The puzzles themselves have a good balance of difficulty and complexity present in the tools available to solve the problem. There isn’t a single place where you’ll have to make a really awkward jump to get through a small gap to grab an item as the game is designed so the difficulty is in the [i]puzzle[/i] and not the platforming abilities of the player. Any “hints” as to where to shoot portals or get to are discreetly displayed within the setting of the world without giving you a set of instructions as to what to do, which is a tricky feat to achieve in level design.

The gameplay is very well thought out in the sense that, the further you get through the game, the more you understand how the cube needs to go on that button that opens that door that released that laser which redirects to those turrets which destroys them giving you access to the spring plate which propels you to the exit. That might seem horribly complicated, but it all makes perfect sense once you understand each individual puzzle item. The game gives you ample opportunity to understand and play with each individual item in its own introductory test - [b]gradually introducing mechanics so in no way are you overwhelmed[/b]. That said, there are no tutorials or hint pop-ups, you are on your own in those 4 walls. This can create problems with players hitting a metaphorical brick wall if they can’t understand or solve something, which is one of the game’s shortcomings. Having said that, like many older style of games, checking a walkthrough guide to get past a tricky section is only cheating if you personally feel it is.

[h2]Writing, Story & Characters[/h2]
Fundamentally, Portal 2 is a puzzle game. But don't let that fool you into thinking this doesn't have an enticing narrative because oh boy does it. The campaign is not just a vehicle to transport the player from one level to the next, the game [i]is[/i] these mid-puzzle story-driven moments that could so easily be a cutscene but instead you get to experience and live through. The story is interactive, one hell of an adventure, and full of all the twists and turns and unexpected moments that will have any player hooked to do just one more chapter. If you played the original Portal, and thought that most of the narrative heavy-work was done through omnipotent voice-over that struggled to form much of an attachment, Portal 2 does a much better job of letting you build a connection with characters that you journey through the world with together. It's less dry sarcastic comments in your ear (though there's still a delightful chunk of that) and more emotional bonding moments that will make you care a lot more both about what happens to you but what happens to the characters and world you encounter. Having said that, the player is still mute, so you don't get much of a say in what happens. The Rattman mini-comic available online serves to bridge the lore-gap between games.

The game doesn't take itself too seriously, there is a lot of humour to be found. A lot of that is silly robots being silly, with an appreciation for how absurd some of the situations you find yourself in are. But while laughing at one character's utter disdain for your personal safety, you might find yourself for a moment fool yourself into thinking that this place really exists out there, somewhere, at some time. [b]The world-building in this game is simply brilliant[/b], while not at all crucial to the main story or to how quickly you can solve puzzles, the care and attention that's gone into making Aperture Science, the portal technology, the facility etc. feel like a real thing with a real history is fantastic. The game is set many thousands of years in the future, and you truly feel when walking the corridors that many a scientist have walked in your footsteps, you wonder to yourself how things got to the way they are, and you notice all the little human things that make you feel a lot more special and important in a world almost entirely inhabited by robots. To further aid that, the vocal performances by J.K. Simmons, Ellen McClain and Stephen Merchant are fantastic, with a script to match.

[h2]Design, Aesthetic & Music[/h2]
The test chambers (where the puzzles mainly take place) vary from extremely large and open to small and claustrophobic but are always simplistic, in other words no matter how elaborate the setting of a puzzle is – and some parts are pretty breath-taking – there’s only a couple important items that you’ll need. In some sections, this can lead to half the puzzle being just locating the special portal-able wall that you need, which is less fun, but the game does an alright job of leading you down the right path. The visual design goes through several phases as the game progresses, but is mainly centred on futuristic tech and electronics, with clean-cut edges and harsh lighting, minimally painted walls and floors with bare metal scaffolding holding the whole thing up. There is also the sense that the world is "alive" in some way. Test elements animate and buzz, wall panels breathe, equipment is transported in and out of the play area. The whole game world feels dynamic and has a certain beauty if you just stand in a spot and observe for a while, which is good, because you'll be doing a lot of that while wracking your brain for the answer to a puzzle.

The music and sound design is impeccable. Putting cubes on buttons and shooting portals sounds incredibly satisfying, even the exit door opening sounds like a [i]"well done"[/i]. Some of my favourite parts of the game are in the manufacturing areas, where the ambience of machinery working away, conveyer belts moving, robots bleep-blooping, pneumatic tubes rushing sounds very real. Furthermore, all of the decorative items in the world, along with some tools that you actually use in puzzles, seem to sing from the same song sheet. That is to say, clearly a lot of care and attention has gone in to making all of these seemingly unrelated sounds work together to produce some very mechanical but strangely beautiful music. This folds like magic into the soundtrack, produced by Mike Morasky, which sounds robotic and distorted and harsh in parts, melodic, rhythmic and synthesizer heavy in others, and lush and orchestral in more still. It truly takes you for a ride, and does as good a job as I've seen in any game of making the dull parts seem less dull and the impactful, dramatic parts even more so. It's also [b]dynamically responsive to what the player does in-game[/b], producing some fantastic moments where it sounds like the music is being arranged and played live, and is far more than just a neat party trick.

[h2]Summary[/h2]
Portal 2 is well worth your time and money. A captivating core gameplay loop that will make you feel far smarter than you deserve, an expansive alternative world to explore littered with fun and interesting details, characters that are multi-dimensional and genuinely funny, music to bop along to that makes your brain work harder and an adventure story with heartfelt emotion, epic battles and daring escapes. [b]Highly recommend.[/b]

[b]Portal 2[/b] expands on the original with deeper mechanics, cooperative puzzle systems, and more complex environmental interactions, making each test chamber a satisfying exercise in physics, timing, and spatial reasoning.

[b]CORE GAMEPLAY MECHANICS[/b]

[*][b]Portal Gun[/b] - Creates interlinked entry and exit points, enabling creative movement, momentum-based puzzles, and emergent problem-solving.
[*][b]Environmental Puzzles[/b] - Test chambers introduce lasers, gels, excursion funnels, and weighted cubes, all interacting predictably with consistent mechanical rules.
[*][b]Physics & Momentum[/b] - Jumping, falling, and launching through portals obey physics, letting players chain actions for inventive solutions.
[*][b]Timing & Sequencing[/b] - Many puzzles require coordinating actions, moving objects, and triggering events in the correct order.

[b]COOPERATIVE MODE MECHANICS[/b]

[*]Two-player co-op introduces dual portals and complementary movement, forcing coordination and shared problem-solving.
[*]Each player’s actions mechanically impact the other, creating emergent teamwork puzzles.
[*]Communication and timing are critical to successfully navigating co-op chambers.

[b]REPLAYABILITY & ENGAGEMENT[/b]

[*]Emergent solutions from consistent mechanics encourage experimentation.
[*]Complex puzzles scale difficulty while reinforcing understanding of core mechanics.
[*]The combination of single-player and co-op keeps mechanical engagement fresh.

[b]10/10[/b] - clever physics puzzles, mechanically rich co-op systems, and inventive environmental interactions make Portal 2 a timeless puzzle masterpiece.

I’ve been playing Counter-Strike for a long time, and right now the biggest issue isn’t the gameplay itself — it’s the matchmaking experience. The level of toxicity in competitive matches is exhausting. Instead of focusing on tactics and teamwork, you often end up dealing with constant insults, screaming, and pointless arguments.

Maybe it’s time to seriously consider stricter age restrictions or some kind of verified age system for competitive matchmaking. In theory, that could reduce the amount of immature behavior in ranked games.

But honestly, I’m not even sure that would fix anything. These days, kids from 8 to 16 can swear and flame harder than most adults. Sometimes it genuinely feels like half the lobby just came straight from Dota, bringing all that chaotic energy with them.

At the same time, I have to admit — CS2 is probably at the peak of its pace and dynamics in the entire history of the game. The speed, the aggression, and the mechanical skill ceiling are higher than ever. The core gameplay feels intense and competitive in the best way possible.

And on a more nostalgic note — I’d honestly love to hear the old knife sounds again. Those classic hits had a special feeling to them. But I also understand that this is probably just nostalgia and a bit of fantasy at this point.

This is just my personal opinion, and I completely understand that others might disagree) But until moderation improves or matchmaking becomes smarter, it’s hard for me to truly enjoy playing with random teammates.

I installed Counter-Strike 2 thinking I was going to have fun.

What I got instead was a highly advanced psychological experiment conducted by Valve to measure how long five strangers can blame each other before someone rage-quits.

The game promises:

“Sub-tick precision”

“Enhanced graphics”

“Improved smoke physics”

What it actually delivers:

Getting one-tapped by someone who appears to be pre-aiming your future grandchildren

Teammates who bought a Negev on pistol round because “trust me bro”

Smokes so realistic you can’t see anything... including your will to win

The ranking system is a masterpiece. You can top frag, entry, clutch twice, plant the bomb, defuse the bomb, solve global warming and still lose 480 rating because your teammate decided to disconnect after round three to “fix his mic.”

Every match follows the same five stages:

Optimism

Confusion

Blame

Copium

“One more game”

Hit registration feels like you’re politely asking the enemy if they’d consider taking damage. Meanwhile, they shoot in your general postcode and you’re instantly back in spectator mode.

And yet… somehow… you queue again.

10/10 worst experience of my life.
See you tomorrow.

Counter-Strike 2 is, without a doubt, a legendary shooter. The franchise has defined competitive FPS gaming for decades, and the core gameplay is still incredibly satisfying. The gunplay feels sharp, the movement is responsive, and the tactical depth is what makes this game timeless. When everything works as it should, CS2 is one of the best competitive experiences you can have.

However, there is a serious issue that’s hurting the game right now — cheaters.

It’s extremely difficult to play more than 2–3 matches in a row without running into someone who is clearly cheating. Wallhacks, aimbots, suspicious behavior — it happens far too often. This completely ruins the competitive integrity of the game and makes grinding Premier or matchmaking feel pointless.

Another problem is Deathmatch mode. Instead of being a solid warm-up environment, it’s filled with AI bots and questionable accounts. It doesn’t feel like a proper practice mode anymore, which is disappointing for players who want to improve.

If someone truly wants to play CS2 seriously, the only real option right now is Faceit. Third-party platforms offer much better anti-cheat systems and a more competitive environment. That alone says a lot about the current state of official matchmaking.

CS2 has legendary potential — the gameplay foundation is amazing. But without strong anti-cheat improvements, many players will continue to feel frustrated.

I really hope the developers take the cheating problem seriously and prioritize fixing it. This game deserves better.

100% classic Battle royal, I've played since release or maybe it was open beta. This battle royal is the roots to many BR's, but it came after H1Z1 and this is how it plays: there are lean mechanics, you can choose games of third person or first, the movements are blocky, but pretty fair and  skill based. The player base is the only downside to the game as the match making isn't fun due to cheaters, robots, or people who've had a lot of hours consistently. There are many game modes and not every game will you face constantly max level players so for the times you don't face cheaters or insane players you have great games that are extremely complex with different ways the fights go down

Example: I've ran over people with vehicles, done drive-by in the vehicles of the game, been killed by people shooting out of the plane vehicles, had enemies and teammates crushed by the "Deployable cover flair" when it drops 2 large cement structures very fast, killed 10 players with crossbows (hard difficulty)(achievement), grenades  of many different varieties (including blue zone grenades - copied from fortnite, but good move), deaths from the many different special weapons that drop from the red crates, and so much more.

One map had a gulag, but i think it's out of rotation now, but they instead also took the concept of being revived by teammates just as other BR's did and that is a good  change.

The game mode of 88 bots and 12 players is the most enjoyable to get warm and ready to face harder opponents. I hope for any of you reading this that you get to play versus people your own level. Whatever you do, dont let your first game be with that lvl 100+  friend... ENJOY IT WHILE YOU CAN.

There is a team deathmatch game mode, it takes place in small circles of random spots on the actual maps so that's awesome for getting warmed up

The games are exhilarating, Balanced well to where all guns are useful, you can choose to play safe, slow, fast, like a rat, or  however you like. Ghillie suits are a thing and they're fun. 

I've only seen 3 bad changes and they were map changes, but the new items added, new vehicles, skins, gameplay (Except the Match Making), emotes, etc... is all pretty great.


Tell me your thoughts?

Started out extremely fun, but the endgame is lacking atm. I do nothing but PvP, so keep that in mind with this review. 

1. If you're descent at the game and bring a great loadout you will be put in skilled PvP lobbies where the loadout is Venator IV + Toro IV. If you're not running Toro you're at a massive disadvantage, it's just too strong. 

2. Every single fight in said lobbies is started or ended with 6 trigger nades. 

3. If you don't run snap hook you are at a massive disadvantage. You should NOT be able to put the snap hook in your safe pocket nor should you be able to swap to a weapon by the time you land. That would immediately balance this. 

3. There are toooooooo many bugs and exploits for an extraction shooter. If you're gear is on the line you shouldn't have to deal with the broken flavor of the week. When something gets fixed after being completely broken for weeks something else is immediately exploited or broken. 

4. The de-sync is out of control on some servers. I solved this mostly by turning cross-play off when I'm ready to sweat. Console timmys seem to be most of the problem here for me, at least. 

5. The PvE side of this game is completely non-existent if you're half descent at video games and kill each enemy type a few times. I honestly don't understand what these people who are pure PvE do for hours in this game. You can only kill a matriarch or a bastion with the same exact strat so many times before you want to gouge your eyes out. 

6. Most importantly, there are almost no quality of life improvements or innovations happening. Rebuilding gear sets and crafting things over and over again is tedious. There are dozens of great ideas online to streamline this, but Embark can barely get ahead of all the bugs in the game so I expect nothing here. 

TLDR: The hype is real and the game was disgustingly fun, but the depth is gone if you don't enjoy playing in the absolute meta and farming the exact same locations every single round. Even with the fun, the bugs and exploits shit on the experience way too hard. Get it on sale when they add a few more maps and weapons and clear out bugs.

PvP players treat this like extraction fortnite. Kill everyone, take it all. Try to make it out with something. Peeking every corner. Setting traps and ambushes. Seems really fun. I just prefer PVE.

Then you have the wildcard players. There is the clip I saw of a guy using a soundboard to make mario sounds when he jumps. There was another guy that is just a combat medic going and healing and rezzing guys. Another guy takes your confessions. I was in stella montis and two guys came up. One had a guitar and another a shaker. They gave me a recorder. We ran around the map playing songs for people. During the last 5 or so minutes we stayed at the last extraction and just kept hitting the button so anyone would have a train ready at a moments notice.

Play this game how you want. Make whatever story for yourself you want to follow. Enjoy the friends you make along the way.

With almost 400 hours on the game, I think I can give an honest review:-

Positives:

1) Incredible graphics, scenery, mechanics, player interaction *potential*.
2) The learning curve and ladder to level 75 is fun.
3) Gameplay and matchmaking was fun - until January 2026.

Negatives:

1) It's boring, repetitive, gameplay and matchmaking is beyond terrible since January.
2) Their aggression-based matchmaking has ruined the dynamics of the game completely. Wish I could get my money back now, even though I've enjoyed all these hours - that's how it feels.
3) Hackers aren't banned instantly. Instead, they're given three strikes.
4) Late game spawns - I understood the concept before aggression-based matchmaking, it was a balance. Now, it's almost pointless in PvE games, and in PvP, it's just not enjoyable at any second. 
5) The "grind-reward" feedback system let's call it - is completely broken since the aggression-based matchmaking came in - in a multitude of dimensions. I'm not sure what the devs/engineers/scientists (if they have any) were thinking, but it lacks all logic.
6) They really need to lower the amount of ARC in this game in certain game modes/maps. It's just becoming annoying, especially when the lobbies are PvP, given that you have 3rd, 4th, 5th and 6th party enemies to deal with.
7) The game feels like it's coming to it's end. 

Sadly, I'm close to uninstalling, but it was good fun till end of 2025.

I truly do not understand the hate for ARC Raiders. This game rules. And yes, you might get absolutely obliterated in the beginning. That’s part of the process. Here’s the secret sauce nobody wants to admit. Let yourself get killed. Over and over. Don’t shoot back. Don’t resist. Just accept death like a raider monk. After about ten deaths, the game basically says “okay, you’re chill” and drops you into the friendliest lobbies known to mankind.

Everyone loves to scream about PvP, but you’re only in PvP if you’re acting like a menace and hunting other players. If you’re not doing that, the vibe completely changes. The friendly lobbies are insane. People are just vibing, looting in peace, handing out blueprints, dropping weapons like it’s a garage sale. No stress. No sweat. Just good raider energy. It feels more co-op than PvP, and it’s honestly hilarious how different the experience is compared to what the angry reviews describe.

If you’re wondering if you can play this game without constantly getting dunked on by PvP tryhards, yes. Absolutely yes. I’ve been doing this for around 100 hours and it’s been amazing the whole time. So don’t let the negative reviews gaslight you into skipping this game. Give it a little time, die with purpose, and you’ll see why ARC Raiders is actually something special.

I’m honestly starting to hate this game.

Every single time I finally secure high-value loot, I get wiped by rats and free-loadout players camping in corners like that’s the entire meta. It’s not skill. It’s not smart play. It’s low-risk behavior that the game actively rewards.

What’s the point of grinding for gear, planning routes, winning fights, and taking real risks if someone with nothing to lose can sit in a dark spot for 20 minutes and delete you in two seconds? That’s not “hardcore.” That’s broken design.

The risk-reward system feels completely backwards. Players who bring real gear and actually engage are punished the hardest. Meanwhile, people running free or disposable kits have zero fear and zero consequence. If they lose, nothing happens. If they win, they walk away stacked. That imbalance ruins the competitive integrity.

Instead of rewarding mechanical skill, smart rotations, and tactical decision-making, the game rewards patience-abusing campers who avoid interaction until the easiest possible moment. It turns intense raids into coin flips. You can do everything right and still lose to someone who contributed nothing to the match except hiding.

That’s not tension — it’s frustration.

A hardcore game should reward risk, skill, and confidence. Right now, it rewards passivity and cheese tactics. The balance feels off, the flow feels stale, and the overall experience feels more unfair than challenging.

If this is the intended gameplay loop, then it’s a serious design problem. Because at this point, it doesn’t feel competitive — it feels punishing for anyone who actually tries to play the game properly.

Fix the risk-reward balance. Stop incentivizing rats. Reward actual engagement.

Until then, this just feels bad.

Toxic PvP players are ruining this game, both with the nastiness they bring to the community and with their "playing style," which mostly consists of waiting in some dark corner and shooting a distracted or wounded player in the back, often right at the point of extract. It's profoundly unbalanced. It allows players who have put in little to no time or effort to take advantage of others who have, with no investment, little to no risk, and no meaningful consequences. It also requires no skill, which is why it's so appealing to a certain type of player.

A game based around the premise of an underground city full of resistance fighters has serious immersion-breaking and narrative defying problems when murderers and thieves are welcomed back with open arms. There should be some sort of "rat faction" for those who wish to play that way.

They can live in unfurnished holes in the ground, deprived of the amenities of Speranza civilization, with no access to traders. They should have limited extraction point options, they should be denied access to certain skins so they're more easily identified, and they should be seen as what they are: the sworn enemies of those who are trying to liberate what's left of civilization from whatever force is sending these killer robots from orbit.

I love 90% of this game. I hate that final 10%--it's just game breaking--and it's why I'm not playing this game in its current state. As it stands now, I'm hoping the developers address the toxicity issues as soon as possible. Toxic player bases kill games. Embark has to know this.

The duplication glitches, the hacking, the cheating has to be addressed, but that's going to happen in any MMO that becomes this popular, and it's only fair to give the developers time to respond and adjust.

But the PvP is incredibly unbalanced, takes no skill, and the vast majority of PvP consists of getting shot in the back and instantly killed without the opportunity to defend yourself. If you do manage to pull a gun before a coward manages to knock you, you'll be sent to PvP lobbies just for defending yourself.

PvP was added very late in the development cycle, it wasn't adequately implemented, and it just doesn't stack up against the rest of the game.

Unfortunately, I couldn't recommend this game in its current state, and I wish I had known about these far reaching problems before purchase. I hope to be able to come back and change this review. We'll see how that goes.

This game is the "perverse incentives" simulator.

For the uninitiated, a perverse incentive in economics is "when the rules, structures, or practices of any system reward bad behavior or sociopathic outcomes (Brownstone Institute)."  As you can probably guess, in this case it involves pvp vs. pve players.

The developers have acknowledged an aggression-based matchmaking (ABMM) system that learns who shoots first at other players, and who doesn't.  It "tends" (emphasis on "tends") to put players with higher aggression scores into matches with the ganker-aligned by raising their aggro score.  Alternatively, players who do not attack other players will eventually end up in "care bear" matches with other players who don't kill on sight and want to, oh I don't know, take down major enemies together or cooperate on objectives.  While theoretically gankers will end up in lobbies where everyone kills everyone all the time and nothing get accomplished.

Herein lies the rub, due to a spectacularly bad design philosophy even defending yourself against PVPers and gankers AFTER THEY HAVE SHOT YOU FIRST gives you aggro score.  So players who get attacked DON'T FIGHT BACK for fear of spending the next 10 matches getting shot on sight, killed by spawn campers, or being attacked as soon as they take down a major enemy (and therefore are low on health or ammunition).  They either submit or run for the exits.  Even if you run, the PVP damage is so high that the person who shoots first can usually down a player in 2-3 shots max.

Scientists in a lab could not design a better perverse incentive.

This ABMM sorting doesn't always happen, and it's easy to game by doing what are called naked runs of doing a free loadout, entering a match, then exiting a handful of times to reset your aggro score.  PVP players know they can attack other players and know the players are unlikely to fight back.

For a lot of gankers, randomly ruining someone else's game is psychotic fun (the boards are full of people writing Nietzschean Cosplay fanfic about how it reveals a truer state of the human condition to spawn camp people who won't fight back).  For a lot of other players, who've maybe worked a long day and don't want to grind the resources necessary to rebuild their kit, it's pure aggravation.  When you die, you lose everything that's on you except for what's stored in the safe pocket (aka the prison purse).  Once you are downed but before you are out of the match, you cannot access your inventory to secure valuables or look at the map to attempt to crawl toward an exit.

Bottom Line: unless and until this game makes it so defending yourself isn't counted as aggression, it's broken.

Pros
1. the atmosphere is great; the music and graphics are very cool

cons:
1. lag lag lag, this is the major problem right now, I have died a few times already due to server lag
2. there is no real way to know who is in the lobby, would be nice to have a screen showing people 
3. they need to remove the joining when a game as already started, not great to come in after 15 minutes has passed already, and you can't leave the match either
4. no lifetime stat leaderboards and no K/D stat either
5. you can't customize your look that well, for instance you can't wear head gear options on a different body suit
6. the inventory system is a complete mess and annoying to manage, basically I just sell everything and use free loadouts and sell the loot to buy more space
7. the city underground feels dull and lacking, all you get is a static room with no real interaction 
8. some of the small flying drones are overpowered for what they are
9. no option to go prone, why on earth we can't is beyond me
10. there is a shuddering/graphical glitch issue when inside buildings and looking at objects close up

OVERALL SCORE: 8.7/10

In my experience in many, many shooters over the years, Arc Raiders managed to find some uncharted territories. The movement and combat style is rugged, but realistic. Firefights have a very intense feel. This applies to both arc and other raiders...

The constant presence of arc makes you play into the PvE element of the game, one way or another. With deadly consequences for ignoring them and valuable loot within, each game is preloaded with a set of "bosses" that provide replayable content and can play a huge part (wanted or not), in PvP fights.

Of course the biggest component of the game is its looter extraction style. For the most part, all of the valuables you can find in game are at stake until the final seconds of an extract. With the value of life so high, Embark incorporated a slew of utility items to help keep you off your hands and knees...each one highlighting a different style of gameplay. Traps can create defensive strongholds while ziplines can make for a great escape. Some grenades can clear a room, while others can strategically block passage.

Every game makes you feel like you're fighting for your life in both a battle of wits and will. And more importantly, you're fighting for that sweet sweet goop.

P.S. Please make the stitcher and kettle stock clip = 15 rounds :)

As background, my experience with FIFA and the like is that I jumped from FIFA 2006 to EA FC 24 and then to EA FC 26. FC 26 suffers from a lot of the same problems as EA FC 24, namely several glaring glitches that make the game incredibly frustrating to play. For instance, the game will randomly experience a catastrophic drop in frame rate making a match practically unplayable. This is especially infuriating in a squad battle or rivals game where you really need the game to perform reliably. I've experienced instances where my custom control settings get corrupted where certain actions simply don't work, like clicking R3 to flick the ball up. Other weird glitches that have not been fixed since FC 24 include  "recommended" graphic settings producing low frame rates, drop down menus of players that have been changed out not disappearing when you start entering the late phases of a match, odd hair color glitches where player and fan models have neon hair colors, and ultimate team games just disconnecting and you being given a loss for the disconnection. A problem unique to FC 26 is the likely AI generated crowd models repeating themselves where you see twins or triplets of different people in the crowds.

         I have yet to take a look at the player career mode for this game (once I do might revisit this review), but I recall FC 24 suffering from the problem of an incredibly boring investment system that had you wasting money on such things as "buy a yacht" and having a lackluster personality system that locked you out of different abilities because you couldn't go back an reallocate points to unlock them. I honestly don't have much faith that things have changed, but again I will return to this review if they have.

         I've played a lot of FC 24 and 26 because I enjoy football. But spending any of your gameplay time mindlessly opening card packs that give you a less than 1% chance to get good quality players, dealing with unacceptable glitches, and a steep learning curve that isn't intuitive to new members of the community make it extremely difficult to recommend this game in good faith. A game series that has been in existence for this long does not have any excuse for being so hostile to the player in its design plagued by negligence and lack of care. The tag line "EA finally listened" should not be a point of pride attached to this game. Instead, fans should take it as damning evidence that this company believes that the bare minimum of listening to the fan base's criticism and feedback is too high a bar for them on a normal day when it is in fact the lowest hanging fruit in the gaming industry.

          FC represents a lot of the worst of what gaming has to offer. I can only hope that they one day gain the wisdom that a game should not be a yearly release if it means putting out a low quality product. But history has shown that having faith in EA is guaranteed to be met with disappointment.

This gaming franchise has gone from by far the best football/soccer video gaming experience to absolute garbage. It's really sad to say having played FIFA since 09 and FUT since 11. The Devs really got my hopes up at the beginning of the game cycle because they were "listening to community feedback." However, as soon as the pro players and everyone who is willing to buy FIFA points complained, they reverted back and completely forgot what they were going differently than the past couple of years.

The game play has gotten so unrealistic and the game holds your hand so much with the AI defending. All of the broken mechanics in this game make it so hard to play and enjoy anymore. I know making a video game realistic especially when it comes to an actual sport because there is so many unpredictable variables, but its like they didn't even try. They just slap on the same name and change the number every year but change nothing with the actual gameplay or mechanics. And don't even get me started on the stupid playstyles. They have completely ruined cards. I remember when getting a card that had all 80s stats meant something, now just need a bronze card with Finesse+ and you can score from anywhere. Playstyles have been the worst addition in recent years. And the power curve still didn't change, like they said it would.

Some ideas that they NEED to do in order to make this game enjoyable again would be:

1. REMOVE playstyles and roles completely (My 90+ CM that has 90+ Passing should be able to make a 10 yard pass, just because they don't have Tiki Taka doesn't mean that their passing stats are irrelevant)
2. Actually make the power curve slower (We don't need a promo every single week, promos are actually killing the game, there are way too many cards in this game anymore. There should only be a handful of promos every game cycle. TOTY, TOTS, TOTT, FS, RTTK, and FUTTIES. TOTW, MOTM, and POTM cards are also completely fine. EVOs, are enough already on top of the millions of other cards that we get, we sill see the same 20 players on everyone's teams already. The only reason as to why we have so many promos is so that they can keep cleaning out everyone's wallets, it's actually so pathetic)
3. Make the gameplay feel responsive and fun again (I'm no coder or software engineer, however, for all the money that this company has, it's mind-blowing as to how this game can never have something that absolutely breaks the game and doesn't ruin it. Every update they "fix" something, but then make the gameplay worse and add two more broken mechanics and then we don't get a patch for 2 months. There are SO many other studios and developers that have WAY LESS people and WAY LESS money and make a better game all round)
4. Bring back the old reward system from champs (make rewards come out on Thursdays again instead of instant gratification, this actually gave you something to look forward to instead of people going out and finishing their champs games and flooding the market, the market is already ruined. Plus when the rewards were on Thursdays, you probably thought you had a terrible weekend league, couple days do bye and now you get your rewards, look you get something good out of them)
5. Balance the Men and Women competing against each other (I'm all for having the women in the game. It adds to much more to the game. However, when comparing stats between the men and women, some stats make absolutely no sense at all. I think that they should have 3 versions for all game modes to compensate for this. I mean, they should have an all men's, all women's, and a combined men's and women's game modes for each of champs, rivals, and squad battles. And yes, I understand that when women were introduced into FIFA several years ago, it was only in kick off, and not many people played that. But, Pina should never be bodying VVD and Rio, that just would never happen IRL)
6. Stop trying to make this an E-Sports game (the gameplay is way too unpredictable to be considered an E-Sports game. You have to have certain that when you take a shot on goal from 10 yards out that it's going to go into the same sport 100 times out of 100. If not then stop and figure out which route you want to take with this game. Either E-Sports or for the casual football/soccer fans)

If they really want to bring bad the joy of this game instead of catering towards E-Sports and the rich, they really need to take a step back and make some changes going forward. Like I said I have been playing this game for over 10 years, but certain decisions have seriously hurt this game. Because I know how good this game could be and it's so frustrating to see and play anymore. So, if you are thinking of getting this game, as of right now, DON'T! Save your money and find something else that can make you feel the same fun and enjoyment. Since video games are supposed to be played for fun and relaxation!

FC 26 delivers one of the most exciting and polished football gaming experiences in recent years. The game shines with fluid gameplay that feels responsive and immersive from the first kick-off. Player movement and ball physics have been refined, making matches feel more realistic and strategic. Whether you’re threading a perfect through ball or defending with precision, the action feels satisfying and dynamic.

Visually, FC 26 impresses with detailed player models, smooth animations, and vibrant stadium atmospheres that bring every match to life. The sound design enhances the experience too — from crowd reactions to in-game commentary that stays engaging without feeling repetitive.

The variety of game modes is another strength. Career Mode gives you meaningful choices as you manage a team’s journey over seasons, while online modes offer competitive challenges that keep you coming back for more. Customization options let you shape your club, players, and strategies to fit your playstyle.

The only thing "Enhanced" is the connectivity issues and bugs. Obviously, it's GTA V, so [i]obviously[/i] I recommend the game itself. I just won't entertain the "Enhanced" version with a good review.

[b][u]Enhanced Pros:[/u][/b]
- [b]Faster offline loading times[/b]
- [b]Animals in Online[/b]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
- [b]Slow transactions[/b]: Every 5 transactions, whether that be buying a car or picking up money from the ground puts you on a 1 minute transaction loop. This feels like the equivalent of getting an unskippable ad when watching a video.
- [b]Robbed by Rockstar[/b]: Sometimes R* likes to do this really funny and epic prank where, when you purchase supplies, they will tell you "Unable to purchase supplies at this time" and then just take your money anyway. Or that cute little moment they have when you finish a sell mission, and they decide to forget that you successfully delivered everything and then only give you half the money because they thought you only did half the deliveries.
[b]Now this is NOT an exaggeration. I have so far had to claim back $5,000,000 from R* Support due to this garbage, which they would charge YOU around £40 for in Shark Cards.[/b]
- [b]Buggy Heists[/b]: Another sweet little "feature" R* has is sometimes when their North Sentinel Island servers have a slight little oopsie and you get disconnected from a heist, they'll decide to completely change how you set up the heist and lock you into a set up you never picked with the lowest possible reward (Casino Heist). 
- [b]Wastes Your Time[/b]: Now, as you know, R* already realises your time means nothing to them. They want nothing more than to waste your time. But this is further [i]enhanced[/i] in the "enhanced" version, with around 1 in 10 of your MC Sales being unpaid. So next time you start a sell mission on your own and spend 40 minutes doing the most mundane task of your life, keep in mind that you might not even get paid for it. How cool is that?
- [b]No Text Chat[/b]: Why? Because having people communicate during missions would make the game playable. R* doesn't like that. So they removed it.
- [b]North Korean Voice Chat Monitoring[/b]: If you even so much as breathe the wrong way with Voice Chat active, prepare for the world's most unintelligent artificial intelligence to ban you. Again, they don't want players communicating with each other, that will be bad for business. Players might band together and make money WITHOUT Shark Cards. R* can't have that happen now can they?

Please keep in mind that when I refer to R*, I'm referring to the absolute clowns that they've put in charge of GTA Online. GTA V itself is an INCREDIBLE game as we all very well know. And so are the rest of their games. But there's one department out there that seems like it's filled by people who just figured out how to print "Hello World." Not to mention that they appear to be running servers from 10,000 BCE. 

Also, before someone says "Improved Graphics", don't. They have a Ray Tracing option that doesn't even work.

GTA V Enhanced - 5/10

First playthrough review time.

The PC version of GTA V is very well made and runs smoothly. I played the enhanced version, which seems better optimized than the base version with enhanced graphics. The game works well even on older hardware, and most settings can be set to high without major problems. It supports both first and third person views, and switching between them works well. The game is large, so preloading it or installing it on an SSD helps reduce long loading times, especially in online mode. Overall, the performance and graphics make the experience on PC impressive.

The single player mode is well designed, with a world that feels alive and detailed, and I finally completed the whole franchise. I played GTA V many years ago, maybe around 10 years back, but I hadn’t finished it at that time. The story allows switching between multiple characters, which adds variety compared to older games in the series. The game world is seamless, with no invisible walls or constant loading screens while exploring. The controls work best with a controller, especially for driving, and while keyboard and mouse options can be fully customized, I play all games using keyboard and mouse only, even though I have an Xbox controller, because I prefer this input.

I have completed GTA V 100%, including all content, as well as every GTA game from Vice City to GTA 4 Complete Edition. However, since my main focus is on competitive esports FPS games, I don’t aim to 100% complete every single-player game. I bought GTA V mainly for the single player experience and haven't played much online.

Overall, the PC version is polished and well executed. The single player story and the seamless open world demonstrate the continued quality and depth of the game, even years after its release.

There are so many things that I could say about this beautiful game which I've enjoyed on and off for several years now.  It truly is a labor of love and the ultimate comfort food for me.  Designing and building a viable farm from the harvestable resources that are available to you is incredibly fun and engrossing and there's something down right magical about how the cycle of the year is depicted and the way that the seasons change the Valley.  In revisiting this game recently, I was surprised to rediscover how dark some of the side storylines are as you get to know more about the villagers and their troubles.  I somehow had forgotten that alongside the cozy, feel-good plot about helping apple-shaped forest sprites restore a run down community center, this game also tries to tackle themes of poverty, homelessness, alcoholism, suicide, and abuse, basically the darker parts that come with living in a small, economically stressed town.  Stardew Valley, as in the setting itself, may be an escape from the tedium of modern life that the player wants and embraces but the same isn't so for some of the other townsfolk who grew up there, particularly the younger and poorer ones who dream of escape in the other direction, leaving the Valley to move into the city.  So all that to say I think an important component of this game is that amidst raising chickens and building beehives, it does try to grapple with some more mature themes, though the storytelling is very simple and sometimes clunky.  It's not just mindless escapism and I respect this game all the more because of that.

Steam says 233 hours. Steam is only telling you about one of my problems. I also own this game on Switch, iPad, and I'm fairly certain if my toaster had a screen I'd own it there too. ConcernedApe could release a Stardew Valley edition for the back of an Etch A Sketch and I'd buy it on launch day. Conservatively I have put thousands of hours into this farming simulator across every device I own and I have never gotten married in it. Not once. Every eligible bachelor and bachelorette in Pelican Town has been waiting for me to give them a bouquet since 2016 and they will continue to wait because I am too busy committing crimes against agriculture.
See, the thing about Stardew Valley is that there are two modes I play it in, and neither of them is the way ConcernedApe intended.
Mode one: I mod it until it's Factorio. Automate the sprinklers. Automate the harvesting. Optimize the crop layouts. Calculate gold-per-tile-per-season ratios. Add industrial machinery mods until my quaint little farm looks like an Amazon fulfillment center that happens to grow parsnips. Grandpa's ghost shows up to evaluate my farm and I'm pretty sure he just cries.
Mode two: I become a wine and cheese oligarch who doesn't even play the game. I install Auto-Sleep, fill every shed with kegs and casks, and then walk away from my computer for three real-world days while my character sleeps through entire seasons generating passive income like some kind of agrarian trust fund kid. I come back, collect my millions, and feel nothing. This is what the American Dream looks like and it's a pixel farmer unconscious in a cabin surrounded by ancient fruit wine.
I have never finished the Community Center the way you're supposed to. I have never seen the endgame content. I couldn't tell you what's at the bottom of the Skull Cavern because every time I go in there I get distracted by a new save file where I'm going to "play it right this time" and then immediately start modding it into an automation nightmare again.
The worst part is ConcernedApe. This man. This single developer who apparently does not require sleep or food. Just when I think I'm finally free, just when the grip loosens and I start to have hobbies again, he drops a point update and the entire internet collectively loses its mind. My feed fills up with "OH MY GOD YOU CAN DO WHAT NOW" and then it's 2am and I'm reading patch notes like scripture and starting yet another farm where I will absolutely not get married and will definitely turn into a wine factory within two in-game weeks.
One guy made this. One. Most AAA studios can't ship a working menu screen with 400 employees and this dude just keeps adding content like he's got a personal vendetta against my free time. It's the best $15 I've spent nine separate times.

Stardew Valley is what happens when you trade fluorescent office lighting for golden pixel sunsets and somehow come out richer for it. You inherit a run down farm, a handful of parsnip seeds, and a town full of people who feel surprisingly real for 16 bit sprites. From there, the game quietly unfolds like a well loved journal.

At its core, it is a farming simulator. You plant crops, raise animals, fish in glittering rivers, and dive into monster filled mines. But that description is like calling pizza “bread with stuff.” The real magic is in the rhythm. Wake up, water crops, talk to the locals, maybe give someone a gift that reveals a little more about who they are. The days move quickly, yet never feel rushed. It is cozy without being shallow.

Pelican Town is packed with personality. Each character has their own struggles, secrets, and little heart events that turn simple conversations into emotional snapshots. You can build friendships, start a romance, get married, and even raise kids. It feels like tending to a garden of relationships, not just crops.

The gameplay loop is addictive in the quietest way. “Just one more day” turns into three in game weeks. There is always something to improve. Upgrade tools, decorate your farm, restore the community center, automate with sprinklers. It scratches that progress itch without turning into a grindy treadmill.

Visually, it leans into charming pixel art that feels nostalgic but intentional. The seasonal changes are especially beautiful. Spring is soft and hopeful, summer hums with energy, fall glows like a campfire, and winter feels peaceful and reflective. The soundtrack ties it all together with gentle melodies that somehow make watering digital turnips feel profound.

If there is a downside, it is that the open ended nature can feel overwhelming at first. The game does not hold your hand. It hands you seeds and says, “Figure it out.” For some players, that freedom is bliss. For others, it may take a few in game weeks to find a groove.

Overall, Stardew Valley is a masterclass in cozy design. It is not about winning. It is about growing. Crops, friendships, skills, and maybe even your own patience. It turns simple routines into something quietly meaningful.

Final verdict: A pixelated sanctuary that proves sometimes the best adventure is planting potatoes and watching them thrive. 🌻

[h1]Stardew Valley – The Game That Brought Me Home[/h1]
[b]Game:[/b] Stardew Valley
[b]Developer:[/b] ConcernedApe
[b]Genre:[/b] Farming Sim / Life Sim / RPG

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Introduction – A Return to Something I Thought I’d Lost[/h2]
Growing up, I spent countless hours playing Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life on the Playstation 2. It wasn’t just a farming game to me—it was routine, comfort, and quiet progression. Feeding animals after school. Watching crops grow day by day. Slowly building a life.

Over time, I drifted away from farming sims. They either felt simplified, rushed, or missing something intangible. Then Stardew Valley appeared—and somehow it didn’t just revive the genre. It revived that feeling.

It reminded me why I loved these games in the first place.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]The Farming – Simple, Deep, and Perfectly Paced[/h2]
At its core, Stardew Valley is about tending to your land. Planting crops, watering them, upgrading tools, raising animals, expanding your farm. But it never feels repetitive.

The loop is satisfying because progression is tangible:
• Early game: scraping by with basic tools and limited stamina
• Mid game: sprinklers, expanded barns, artisan goods
• Late game: efficient layouts, gold-star harvests, optimized production

It captures that same steady growth that A Wonderful Life did—but with more flexibility and player freedom. You can min-max, or you can casually grow pumpkins and fish all day. The game supports both.

And that’s beautiful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Pixel Art – Warm, Timeless, Emotional[/h2]
The pixel art in Stardew Valley is nothing short of charming. It’s colorful without being overwhelming. Soft without being dull. Seasonal transitions feel magical.

Spring feels alive.
Summer feels vibrant.
Fall feels cozy.
Winter feels quiet and reflective.

There’s a warmth to the visuals that makes the town feel lived in. You don’t just see Pelican Town—you feel it.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Characters – Small Stories That Feel Real[/h2]
One of Stardew Valley’s greatest strengths is its writing. Every character feels like they have layers.

• People struggling with identity
• People stuck in routine
• People grieving
• People chasing dreams
• People learning to open up

The heart events aren’t just cute cutscenes. They explore loneliness, depression, family tension, ambition, insecurity. It’s subtle, but it hits.

Building relationships doesn’t feel transactional—it feels gradual and human.

That’s rare.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Music – Pure Nostalgia, Pure Comfort[/h2]
The soundtrack is unforgettable. It balances calm melodies with uplifting seasonal themes.

Some tracks feel hopeful.
Some feel peaceful.
Some feel nostalgic before you even realize why.

There are moments in Stardew Valley where you’re just standing on your farm at sunset, music playing softly, and it hits you: this is what relaxation feels like.

The soundtrack carries emotion without demanding attention.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Freedom – Play Your Way[/h2]
Stardew Valley doesn’t force you into one playstyle.

You can focus on:
• Farming
• Fishing
• Mining
• Animal raising
• Artisan goods
• Relationships
• Community Center completion
• Exploration and secrets

It never punishes you for going at your own pace. There’s no urgency. No ticking clock pushing you forward. It respects your time.

That design philosophy makes it timeless.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]How It Brought Me Back[/h2]
After years away from farming sims, Stardew Valley felt like coming home.

It carried the spirit of Harvest Moon: A Wonderful Life—the slow growth, the emotional warmth, the routine—but refined it with modern design, deeper mechanics, and player freedom.

It didn’t just modernize the genre. It reminded me why I loved it.

That’s powerful.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Why It’s a 10/10[/h2]
[b]Farming Mechanics:[/b] 10/10
[b]Pixel Art:[/b] 10/10
[b]Character Writing:[/b] 10/10
[b]Music:[/b] 10/10
[b]Replayability:[/b] 10/10
[b]Emotional Impact:[/b] 10/10

[b]Overall: 10/10[/b]

Anglo-French Wars
The Hundred Years' War (French: Guerre de Cent Ans; 1337–1453) was a conflict between the kingdoms of England and France and a civil war in France during the Late Middle Ages. It emerged from feudal disputes over the Duchy of Aquitaine and was triggered by a claim to the French throne made by Edward III of England. The war grew into a broader military, economic, and political struggle involving factions from across Western Europe, fuelled by emerging nationalism on both sides. The periodisation of the war typically charts it as taking place over 116 years. However, it was an intermittent conflict which was frequently interrupted by external factors, such as the Black Death, and several years of truces.

The Hundred Years' War was a significant conflict in the Middle Ages. During the war, five generations of kings from two rival dynasties fought for the throne of France, then the wealthiest and most populous kingdom in Western Europe. The war had a lasting effect on European history: both sides produced innovations in military technology and tactics, including professional standing armies and artillery, that permanently changed European warfare. Chivalry reached its height during the conflict and subsequently declined. Stronger national identities took root in both kingdoms, which became more centralized and gradually emerged as global powers.[2]

The term "Hundred Years' War" was adopted by later historians as a historiographical periodisation to encompass dynastically related conflicts, constructing the longest military conflict in European history.[3][4] The war is commonly divided into three phases, separated by truces: the Edwardian War (1337–1360), the Caroline War (1369–1389), and the Lancastrian War (1415–1453). Each side drew many allies into the conflict, with English forces initially prevailing; however, the French forces under the House of Valois ultimately retained control over the Kingdom of France. The French and English monarchies thereafter remained separate, despite the monarchs of England and Great Britain styling themselves as sovereigns of France until 1802.

Origins
The root causes of the conflict can be traced to the crisis of 14th-century Europe. The outbreak of war was motivated by a gradual rise in tension between the kings of France and England over territory; the official pretext was the interruption of the direct male line of the Capetian dynasty.

Tensions between the French and English crowns had gone back centuries, since the Norman Conquest of 1066 had put a king of (Norman) French origins, William, duke of Normandy, on the throne of England. Since that time, English monarchs had held titles and lands within France, which made them vassals to the kings of France. The status of the English king's French fiefs was a significant source of conflict between the two monarchies throughout the Middle Ages.[citation needed] According to military historian and author Michael Livingston, the conflict began in 1337, when Philippe VI of France claimed that France controlled English holdings in France.[5]

In 1328, Charles IV of France died without any sons or brothers, initiating a succession crisis. A similar crisis in 1316 had resulted in the Estates-General in 1317 deciding that "Women do not succeed in the kingdom of France". Charles's closest male relative was his nephew Edward III of England, whose mother Isabella was Charles's sister. Isabella claimed the throne of France for her son by the rule of proximity of blood, but the French nobility rejected this on the basis of the 1317 decision, declaring that Isabella could not transmit a right she did not possess. An assembly of French barons decided that a native Frenchman should receive the crown rather than Edward.[6]

The throne passed to Charles's patrilineal cousin instead, Philip, Count of Valois who had been made regent on the death of Charles IV. Edward protested but ultimately submitted and did homage for Gascony. Further French disagreements with Edward induced Philip during May 1337 to meet with his Great Council in Paris. It was agreed that Gascony should be taken back into Philip's hands, which prompted Edward to renew his claim for the French throne, this time by force of arms.[7]

Edwardian phase
In the early years of the war, the English, led by King Edward III and his son Edward the Black Prince, saw resounding successes, notably at the battles of Crécy (1346) and Poitiers (1356), where King John II of France, having succeeded his father Philip from 1350, was taken prisoner.

Caroline phase and Black Death
By 1378, under King Charles V the Wise and the leadership of Bertrand du Guesclin, the French had reconquered most of the lands ceded to King Edward in the Treaty of Brétigny (signed in 1360), notably reducing English control on the continent, leaving them with few cities.

However, both countries faced challenges and problems. The Black Death, a deadly plague that spread through Europe between 1347 and 1351 caused catastrophic widespread damage. In France, 6 to 12 million people died, 30% to 60% of the population,[8] resulting in major labour shortages, economic collapse, and widespread social dislocation. England also suffered from the Black Death, but to a lesser extent, with roughly 2–3 million deaths. Economic consequences of the plague and the war led to major unrest in both kingdoms, widespread poverty, and a weakening of royal authority.[9][10] These crises were resolved in England earlier than in France.

Baldurs Gate 3 offers a vast and inviting world in the Dungeons and Dragons universe. You are empowered to choose your way to play this game. You have the option to approach a questline on different ways (negotiate, battle through hords of enemies or sometimes even skipping boss fights, stealth etc). The story is engaging and your allies and foes have well developed personalities. The world is enormous and detailed. Everything in Baldurs Gate 3 cries for endless oportunities and game of the year.

And truth to be said, that is the reason why I could not recommend it. This game is not for everyone, because it is so gigantic and overextending. It binds you for hundreds of hours in front of your computer. And as soon as you complete the game for the first time, you have to play it once again, because you will not grasp every facette of the game by playing it once. For many players this is no problem and will appeal them. You gain a lot of content for a good price. Hoever for a hard working person with de facto little to no free time, Baldurs Gate 3 is too much, too enormous and too long.

Some games ask you to save the world.
Baldur’s Gate 3 politely hands you a tadpole, ruins your mental stability, and then says, “Good luck, champ.”

This game doesn’t just have characters. It has personalities. The kind that make you forget you’re holding a controller and not just binge-watching the greatest fantasy drama never aired on HBO. The voice acting? Absolutely criminal. It’s so good it makes other RPGs sound like they were recorded in a bathroom with a potato. Every conversation feels cinematic. Every line delivery hits.

And then there’s Lae'zel — possibly my favorite personality in the game. She’s rude. She’s intense. She treats kindness like it’s a contagious disease. And her inability to understand sarcasm is pure gold. After a fight with Shadowheart, Shadowheart asks, “Have we buried the hatchet?” and Lae’zel, with the confidence of someone who has never encountered a metaphor in her life, responds: “No. Why should it be buried? Is it broken?”

That moment alone deserves an award.

You can feel the developers poured passion and love into this game. Every quest, every tiny interaction, every weirdly specific dialogue option screams: “Yes, we thought about that too.”

Now let’s talk about the Dark Urge origin. Playing as the Dark Urge is like letting intrusive thoughts win — but narratively. It twists the entire story in ways that are both hilarious and horrifying. I laughed. I gasped. I questioned my fictional sanity. It’s like the game looks at you and says, “You wanted choices? Oh, I’ll give you choices.”

The combat system is chef’s kiss. Turn-based, yes — but so flexible and creative that you can basically weaponize the environment itself. Push enemies off cliffs. Set the ground on fire. Throw random objects because you can. It’s tactical, chaotic, and deeply satisfying. You’re not just fighting — you’re improvising.

Playing with friends? Absolute chaos in the best way. It genuinely feels like playing tabletop Dungeons & Dragons, except the dungeon master has a massive budget and motion capture. The random decisions people make mid-conversation are comedy gold. Someone’s trying to negotiate peace, someone else steals a fork, and suddenly you’re in combat with half the town. Beautiful.

The story and lore are ridiculously well made. Even if you’re new to turn-based games, this is a must-try. The world pulls you in and refuses to let go — politely at first, then violently if you pick the wrong dialogue option.

The in-game modding menu makes it effortless. You don’t like something? Fix it. Add to it. Break it responsibly. On top of that, third-party support has exploded past 16.000 mods and counting. This game isn’t just alive — it’s evolving.

Don’t like the UI? There’s a mod.
Want new subclasses? There’s twenty.
Think the game needs more hairstyles, dice skins, armor sets, or completely unbalanced spells? Done.

And then there are the mods I would absolutely never install… but respect deeply.

Like turning every character into a goblin.
Or replacing dragons with Thomas the Tank Engine.
Or adding a romanceable mind flayer with voice lines that whisper aggressively supportive affirmations.
Or the mod that makes everyone absurdly muscular for no narrative reason.
Or the one that gives Withers a disco outfit and a permanent dance animation.

Would I use them? No.
Am I glad they exist? Absolutely.

That’s the beauty of it. If something bothers you — difficulty spikes, inventory clutter, camera angles — you can just download a mod and move on. The game bends without breaking. That kind of longevity means Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t going anywhere. It’s going to age like fine wine… or like a cursed artifact that only grows stronger over time.

The bad?

Honestly… not much. The dice can be a little annoying. Nothing humbles you faster than failing a 90% chance roll in front of your companions. But even that becomes part of the charm. You’re writing your own story — whether you accept your fate like a hero or shamelessly save scum like the rest of us.

10/10. I genuinely wish more developers cared about crafting games like this. Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t just a great RPG — it’s a love letter to storytelling, player choice, and the beautiful chaos of rolling dice when your life depends on it.

It's frankly, an amazing game. Especially with the vast quantity of mods available in-game and on nexus mods. If you like Dungeons and Dragons, you'll love this game. If you like narrative games, you'll love this game. If you don't like turn based games, exploring, having choices that make a difference and you don't have the patience to follow through a story and play through multiple times and think inventively, you'll hate this game.

Absolutely one of the best games I've ever played. My only complaints are: the game barely ever auto-saves so you will find yourself spending a load of time just saving after fights and major exploring because you don't want to risk having to redo everything either because of a bad choice, an accident, or a crash.  There are a few glitches here and there which can be annoying like the fact that often stored items don't "bunch up" properly so that can be a bit of a mess to organize, or the Act 2 rat fight which glitched out for me like 3 times in a row (and a few more). Lastly, without a guide a lot of the content for your first playthrough is simply a mystery (and by a lot I mean for the vast majority of the time you will have no idea what the long and short terms consequences are) which can "ruin" your playthrough. You can chalk this up to the developers trying to have the game feel more immersive however missing some O.P. items or having characters die simply because you had no clue there was an order in which you had to do certain missions/interactions can be irritating. Apart from that the combat is dynamic and engaging, the enemies are quite different, the map is beautiful and fun to explore, the stories are well written and the voice actors did a phenomenal job! Honestly a 9/10 experience and very easy to replay thanks to the vast amount of different choices and options available in the game.

[h1] A game set apart. [/h1]

Where do I even begin with a game like this? It's praises have been sung from the highest of mountain peaks. Not to mention, it's already been almost 3 years since its release (at the time of writing this review). I probably have nothing to add that you haven't heard before, but I just can't shake the compulsion of an almost duty-like pull to honor this game still. In an age of money hungry corporations taking over our beloved medium, Baldur's Gate 3 stands out for delivering a top quality game at a fair price, and not asking for anything further than the price on the box (or steam page). [b] The short of it, buy this game and support this studio. [/b]

[h3] The long(ish) of it [/h3]

This game is a masterclass in many fronts. From detailed and consistent worldbuilding and lore, to loveable characters with real depth and meaning. There is almost no area in this game where you can say [i] "I wish they thought of this as an option" [/i] because chances are, they did. There is so much attention to detail, and love for gaming and gamers on display in this title. I'd argue that it's impossible to play this game and not feel that the people who made it were having a blast doing so. It's funny, sophisticated, raunchy, emotional, strategic, and so much more.

I had never played an RPG of this style of gameplay, with the more top-down(ish) view and turn based combat, and I will admit, it took a brief period of getting used to. But once I got it, I was hooked. The gameplay is engaging and presents so many ways of handling various situations, that there is always a way out of trouble if you have a bit of imagination. The various classes and multi-classing that the game has allows you to make your playstyle unique and cater to how you want to play. You can approach various encounters with different ways of weapon combat, magic, spells, stealth, wordcraft, deception, and so many more.

The story weaves many narrative threads across three acts and while some resolve in earlier acts, the late game tales are astounding. I was engrossed and always eager to explore every in of a new area to see that I could find, and how it pushed me along the quests of the game. 

Characters were always interesting and compelled me to learn what makes them who they are, and how I can help (or hinder) them from achieving their goals in this world. None of the main cast were 'one-dimensional' or 'typical archetypes' once you got to their core. How invested you become in a character can be up to you, and how you decide to approach their individual quest lines.

There is no shortage of secrets to find, loot to collect, characters to befriend (or foe), stories to unravel, skills to master, and memories to make that will last for a long time to come. Baldur's Gate 3 is a very special game, and I can wholeheartedly encourage anyone interested to take the plunge and dive head first into this wonderful world.

Baldur's Gate 3 is mandatory gaming. I don't care if you "don't like turn-based combat." Try it anyway. This game will change your mind.
The world feels genuinely alive. Maps are dense with secrets and environmental storytelling, and almost every conversation has multiple solutions. You're not on rails. You're actually role-playing.
The companions are incredible. Shadowheart and Gale are standout characters with real depth and development that unfolds naturally over dozens of hours. The writing never feels like it's pandering or hitting checkboxes. These feel like actual people with motivations beyond serving your story.
Combat is tactical and satisfying. The 5E ruleset translates beautifully, and the environmental interactions add layers that tabletop can't match. Shoving enemies off cliffs never gets old.
The one real issue: Act 3. The game needed another act to properly pace the endgame. Act 3 dumps too much content on you at once, and some threads feel rushed while others overstay their welcome. It's still good, but the cracks show compared to the near-perfection of Acts 1 and 2.
Even with that flaw, this is one of the best RPGs ever made. Larian set a new standard. Play it.

The premise of this game allows players to adhere to many of the facets found in D&D 5e.  BG3 accomodates players with an involved storyline.  The differences between a RPG and BG3 is minor.  However, an RPG's story can go through traumatic shifts due to player/character behavior.

The interface is relatively easy to grasp which helps to promote the immersion players feel.  The interface adopts many of the rules found in the 5e ruleset with modifications made to help keep players engaged with the story and plot twists.  Many minor details are missing which even the 5e rules don't focus on like encumberance.  However, details that would only add complexity and make the game a chore to play were purposely left out.  This allowed Larian to keep the focal point on crafting content players can enjoy playing repeatedly and enjoying with new pleasure even when they've seen much of the same content.  Other games need to look at BG3 as a winning model and start designing with the same properties.
