Honestly, I’ve played a lot of games and a lot of RPGs, but when it came to Baldur’s Gate… after a while I realized I was standing against something I had never encountered before. A challenge. A very complex challenge. And since I like challenges, I definitely didn’t back down. Let’s be honest — nowadays you don’t really have to use your brain much when playing games. Developers practically make idiot-proof experiences… but not Larian Studios.

Warning: spoilers and potential mind-blow.

The story itself is a bit more complicated, so I’ll try to explain it briefly. You are a person who has been abducted by so-called Mind Flayers, who implanted a tadpole inside you. That tadpole will eventually transform you into one of them — all in the name of the Absolute… well, in the name of a higher power. Along your journey, you meet other poor souls who also carry a tadpole inside them, and you all share the same goal… well… not exactly. Some of them have their own “personal goals” they want to achieve as well. Whether you like it or not, allies will be extremely useful at the end of the game. But to keep them from leaving you, you need to make sure they feel good around you, follow their personal questlines, and help them complete their own stories. Sometimes it’s not easy. Sometimes it’s frustrating. But trust me — it pays off. Unless you make a mistake. Your companions won’t be fighting in their underwear either. Just like you, they need proper gear — specific armor and weapons suited to them. Obviously, you wouldn’t give a wizard a sword… well… you could, but then I’d love to see those spells.

But seriously, your companions should wear armor appropriate for their class. I still haven’t found a companion who can wear Heavy Armor without locking themselves out of their spells — and that’s important. Whenever you equip a companion with a new piece of armor, check its description carefully. If there’s a small exclamation mark in the tooltip, take that armor off. Otherwise, they won’t be able to use their spells and abilities.

Every character should have a proper weapon, the right armor (or modded gear — that’s up to you), and also a crossbow or a bow. Some can use a shield as well, but that depends on how you want to build them.

Your main goal is to reach Baldur’s Gate… well… what a surprise, right? You want to remove the tadpole and live normally again. Honestly, the story is massive, but Steam doesn’t have a large enough character limit for me to explain it all, so let’s move on.

If you’ve played The Witcher or Life is Strange (that LiS mention is a joke, okay?) then you know that your decisions matter… but here, the game slaps you in the face in a way you’ve probably never experienced before. Your decisions matter a lot. Like… you make one choice, walk into a town, and suddenly you’re in combat because you insulted an NPC who has a friend, and that friend has an army, and that army kicks your ass and you have to reload your save. So yes — remember F5 for Quick Save and F8 for Quick Load. You’ll thank me later.

Seriously, be careful what you say and how you behave. It can help you — or hurt you badly and keep you stuck somewhere much longer than you’d like. I have to admit, I’ve never seen such a well-crafted decision system. At the same time, it can be frustrating when you either have to agree to something you don’t want to… or technically have a choice, but none of the options end well for you.

Your decisions also affect how your companions see you. And if you want to romance one of them, you’d better watch your words and actions. Most people probably fall in love with Shadowheart immediately — the best character I’ve ever met (sorry, Yennefer…). Also… under no circumstances let any of your companions leave. Again — you’ll thank me at the end.

This game also has combat… well, you’re not playing cards for life and death here, are you?

The combat system is… okay, I’ll say it — similar to Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. Yes, you can whip me now. The reason I compare it is because it’s turn-based. Each character has limited movement and actions per turn. You can move a certain distance and usually attack once per turn. And this triggers a beautiful thing called thinking. Yes, exactly. Combat isn’t about waiting until all enemies are dead — you actually have to consider every move and decide who to focus on. And you should save before every fight. Personal experience.

And honestly… I’ll say it for the last time, okay? I finished Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 on New Game+, where enemies are more aggressive and faster and you really have to think or you’ll repeat the whole fight. But I’ve never experienced a combat system as difficult as this one. This is the hardest combat I’ve seen so far. Or maybe it’s just my brain pulling the “Gone fishing” card every time a fight starts and I insist on doing things my way. Still, every fight feels rewarding. Or at least most of them.

I don’t personally think games like this should release too often — it might actually fry my brain because I don’t think I have the mental capacity for RPGs this advanced. But it’s a very welcome change.

There’s also alchemy. If you played the first Witcher, it’s almost the same interface and a similar system — nothing too complicated. However, alchemy is mostly pointless. Most potions you can craft can also be bought from regular merchants for a few gold coins, which makes the whole feature feel unnecessary. Honestly, it kind of is. The only time I used it was to craft healing potions. You can also find scrolls with various spells, which is great and very useful. They can help you through tough sections or even entire fights, and I really appreciated that.

What’s truly key in this game is exploration. The game assumes you’re not stupid and that you can find clues on your own. Many quests don’t even have quest markers telling you where to go or what to do. You have to explore — and most importantly, READ BOOKS. A lot of information is hidden in texts and environmental storytelling. If you expect everything to be served on a silver platter, this probably isn’t the game for you. Personally, I had to get used to this. But after some time, it becomes natural and even meaningful.

Baldur’s Gate excels in many areas. For me, it feels like a combination of The Witcher, Clair Obscur, and Sekiro — Sekiro mainly because some enemies caused me the same kind of pain. Overall, this is a truly impressive game that every RPG fan should try. Its elegance lies in how simple it seems at first — only to surprise you with mechanics that leave you speechless. And it’s definitely not a one-time experience.

If the game really hooks you — like it did with a certain unnamed person — you’ll gladly replay it with a different approach, try new paths, or behave completely differently. Overall, I think this game had enormous potential and squeezed every last drop out of it. Nothing went to waste.

(No wonder it deserved the Game of the Year award.)

I highly recommend this game as one of the must-plays in gaming history. This game coming out did more to push gaming forward as a medium than any game in the last several years. 

That being said...
- The game is a buggy mess. Several quests didn't finish for me and the NPCs literally disappeared. Just as well, several of the boss fights bugged out where the bosses couldn't act in combat. 
- The game is too easy. I played on Tactician + Honor (custom difficulty with everything cranked up) and after just a few levels it's very easy to break the game apart. 
- There's just too many "trash fights" and too many fights in general. DnD (imo) is a problem-solving game, not a medieval fight simulator.
- To the above comment, I can't stand 5e. This isn't really a dig against this video game, but the pandering coupled with the overall design and aesthetics of modern DnD are garbage. 
- I found the art style to be "too much" -- I'd prefer something lower fidelity with more style (a la divinity OS/2). With the high fidelity plus the conversations being so intimate (face to face rather than top down) it makes the pacing feel off when switching between gameplay and exposition.
- As in most RPGs and cRPGs, there are a few really big difficulty spikes or unclear puzzle fights that without prior knowledge/a guide would be too much for most new players. 
- Lastly, this game is obviously highly replayable, but I am so utterly fatigued by my first playthrough I can't fathom replaying it any time soon (as much as I'd love to do a solo honor playthrough for the achievements). It overstays its welcome in favor of "trash" combat rather than exposition and problem solving. There are also 0 downsides to having camp be full, so it pushes you to recruit anyone and everyone regardless of alignment/decision-making.

Despite all my critiques, I am sure I will come back for another playthrough, it just probably won't be for a few years. 

Pick this one up and see why this is a cultural phenomenon and a crowning achievement in the gaming medium.

Baldur’s Gate 3 is one of those rare games that completely pulls you into its world. I honestly haven’t felt this immersed in an RPG since Dragon Age: Origins.

What really stands out is how much the game makes you think. It’s not just about combat or builds — it constantly makes you consider your next move, your next dialogue choice, your next approach. I often found myself thinking about what I’d do differently on the next playthrough while I was still in the middle of the current one. Very few games manage to create that kind of pull.

I completed one campaign with a friend and another solo, and both experiences were incredible in their own way. Co-op added chaos, creativity, and unexpected moments, while the solo run felt more personal and strategic. What impressed me the most was how different things felt the second time around — new paths, different solutions, and completely different outcomes. Even familiar situations played out in new ways depending on my choices and approach.

Playing on Tactician and then Honour Mode (the second hardest difficulty) really pushes you to engage with the systems properly. Positioning, preparation, resource management — everything matters. It feels challenging, but fair and extremely rewarding.

The world, characters, writing, and freedom of choice all come together in a way that makes this game something special. It’s one of those RPGs that stays in your head even when you’re not playing.

It took me a while to actually get BG3 after seeing people rave about Astarion when it initially released, but now that I've actually gotten to play BG3 and complete the storyline, all the praise is definitely earned! I really liked how interconnected all the quests are and how closely tied the companions' quests are to the main storyline as well. 

There's so much content in the game that it took me about 180 hours to even get through both the main storyline and all the sidequests because I spent so much time going from place to place doing every possible quest. So if you're the kind of person who enjoys games that have tons of things to do, then BG3 has no shortage of sidequests. I honestly really appreciated how much content there is, especially since games can get boring pretty quickly if the main storyline doesn't take that long to finish. I was super invested in the story, so I didn't mind at all how long it took to complete.

The companion questlines are also really great and I loved how even if you only pursue friendships with the companions, there's still a lot of depth to the relationships you can form with them. The voice acting far exceeded my expectations as well! You can genuinely tell how much love and care the VAs put into every line. (Neil Newbon definitely won those awards for voicing Astarion for a reason, LOL!)

In my opinion, BG3 is definitely worth the full price, although I got it at a discount myself -- but that was mostly because I planned to get it during the 2025 Winter Sale so I could save a few extra dollars for some other games I'd been eyeing. Either way, the game is worth every penny!

If you had told me I’d spend 60 hours in Act 1 alone, I wouldn’t have believed you—but that’s the magic of Baldur’s Gate 3. After dozens of hours explored, I can confidently say this is the best RPG I have ever played.

Larian Studios has created something that feels less like a video game and more like a living, breathing world that actually reacts to your presence.

Total Player Freedom
The sheer volume of choices is staggering. I’ll be honest: it’s overwhelming at times, but in the best way possible. Every time I think I’ve found the "right" way to solve a problem, I discover three other paths I could have taken. Your decisions don't just change the ending; they ripple through every conversation and combat encounter.

Characters You Actually Care About
The writing here is on another level. Every companion is:

Well-written: They have distinct voices, complex moralities, and deep backstories.

Engaging: I found myself genuinely invested in their approval and their personal growth. They aren't just stat blocks for combat; they feel like a real party.

Unmatched Depth
The fact that I’ve put 60 hours into the opening act and still feel like I’m just scratching the surface is a testament to the content density. There is no "filler" here—just secrets, stories, and surprises tucked into every corner of the map.

The Verdict: > It is rare to find a game that respects the player's intelligence and curiosity this much. If you love storytelling and true agency, this isn't just a "must-play"—it's a masterpiece.

Few titles command your attention like Baldur’s Gate 3. From the opening moments of the campaign, the game pulls you into a narrative that feels remarkably personal. Unlike games that offer only the illusion of choice, Larian Studios has crafted a world where every decision, from a casual dialogue exchange to a major tactical gamble, ripples through the entire journey in unexpected ways.
The attention to detail is nothing short of staggering. Whether it’s the way the environment reacts to your spells or the subtle, motion-captured flickers of emotion on a companion’s face, the world of Faerûn feels alive.
Perhaps the most telling sign of its quality is how easily the countless hours drift away. You sit down to "just finish one more task," and suddenly, the clock has jumped forward half a day. The tactical depth of the combat, combined with the immense emotional weight of the character arcs, creates an addictive loop of exploration and discovery.

Boy I love this game. I became obsessed with it as soon as I started playing.

The characters are amazing, it's incredible how much personality they have, and the voice actors clearly love their jobs. It's so refreshing to see an AAA game made with love, and it deserves every award it got. 
The story is great, and despite the game being incredibly long, it was absolutely worth getting to the end. 
The graphics are also incredibly impressive, and I adore how the first (pre rendered) cutscene looked – it was like watching a movie.
My only gripe is the character creation – it felt a bit limited, but I also understand how hard it would be to make it more complicated and there's nothing mods can't fix. It's good enough for me and I appreciate the different gender options.

Also, one more addition: do not play it for 10 hours straight every single day like I did, and remember to take breaks. It may probably seem obvious to you, but for a long time I found it hard to put the game down because I desperately wanted to see how it ends, while still exploring every area I could. It got exhausting after a while, especially during chapter 3 which had a lot of tedious side-quests. In my second playthrough, I took my time and didn't rush, which made it ten times more enjoyable. 
Overall, 10/10.

I don’t even know what to say about this game.
I’d love to call it perfection, but I know Larian can cook up something even better, so I’ll hold back a bit.

Still, if you want a game full of meaningful choices, great NPCs, strong voice acting, and real consequences, this is absolutely the one for you. It supports both Vulkan and DirectX, is well-optimized, and even runs on Linux.

On top of that, you get one of the best female casts to romance: Minthara, my beloved drow; Shadowheart, my beloved half-elf (and yes, you can even have a threesome with her and Halsin); and Mommy Karlach. There’s even a brothel if that’s your thing.

And if you ever wonder, “Is Baldur’s Gate really that good?” just look up the ridiculous number of awards it has won—and is still winning in 2026.

Anyway, just look at my hours played—this game really took me for a ride. There’s a ton to do.

Starts really strong, amazing freedom, many options to solving tasks. But the deeper the game goes, the less options for problem solving are available.

And closer to end game it just becomes an on-rail type of experience where you can do things in exactly  1 specific way. Which sucks a lot. I level up, get more skills and spells and then the game just freaks out when I dare to use them. 
Oh, you want to use Blink(a spell literally designed for increased survival) for an endurance gauntlet? 
WRONG!

Oh, you want to just assault the bad guy when he taunts you? 
Act 1 = yup, go ahead, it's okay
Act 3 = WRONG! Now everyone is hostile to you

Oh, you follow the logical path in a quest?
WRONG! You should do what journal tells you to do and the logical path just breaks the quest.

Also for some reason in the end game the game tries to force you to use stealth. The only problem is that stealth in this game is pretty bad as far as I can understand. It's a skill, so the higher it is, the harder for enemies to spot you, just like in table top, right? Wrong, if you're in the line of sight, you are seen, if you are outside of line of sight, you are hidden. The skill does nothing.

But the biggest offence - this game doesn't have Xanathar spells and subclasses even though it has the lame bladesinging from Tasha.

Hear ye', hear ye', Baldur's Gate 3 review for thee, from RPG enjoyer of me.

When I said I want to play RPG games, it's not just about having varied builds, class, or a lot of perks tree skills, but what I want is a roleplaying immersion from gameplay and dialogue. Definitely the latter, I've played Kingdom Come and Witcher for that solely reason, to have my own approach dialogue, given as many options I can do to resolve a conflict, respecting me either it's a "bad" decisions or "good". I love that this game fulfilled the desire of playing a good RPG game.

To have so many dialogue options that unlocks different path from the first solution is just so fun! Many games will just give you "yes" or "no", but this game give you "5 W + 1 H" and "yes" or "no"  options. Because many conflicts need to be dug down more and I need to observe more, I can't be too judgy at the start. And in gameplay manner, there are many approach like books or items and different NPCs POV (even pets!) you can interact with that will be added to dialogue perspective, reveal more options and having the best solution. And I love that sooooo much. The choices can be harsh and filled with dilemma, but let's be real, the game is generous enough for me to save before progressing with the dialogue, leaving with safer outcome where, If I messed up or don't like the solution, I gotta go back. Many quests are like that, where I believe, having silver tongue is better than solving things in combat. Well, because the combat is so hard to understand.

Don't get me wrong, I really am not familiar with the combat mechanic. When the game says turn-based-combat, my brain will think something like final fantasy 7 or recent game like Expedition 33, where combat and exploration are in different section. Well, jokes on me, the combat is in real-time, WHAT?! I didn't know that. I'm just saying that early gameplay curve was really was high where the game overwhelmes me, both gameplay and mechanic. I don't know how to play, I don't know what to press, which skills I have to press, what is concentration, uhh spell slots, 1, 2, 3? More worse, I don't even know what my character role. Even I was in despair time and googling on internet like, "how to beat these, it's too hard". One of the solution that open my eyes is, "use the environment". After that, I forgot that this game give me so many freedoms to approach everything in combat such as high ground, stealth, surprised, and one of my favorite thing to do, push them out to cliff (best solution). I realized that after mid-game, this freedom is really fun. Unlike other game that force you to fight your way through, I don't like that, I want to stealth, and the game respect me to it. One time the boss fight swarmed with many enemies and traps before the main room and I just went stealth bypassing everything maximazing the gameplay mechanic like flying, teleporting, stealth, and even I became a gas once to positioning, my God this game is really fun!

Better yet, this combat gameplay are actually contemplating with dialogue approach where, at first I didn't know, but I can spare them somehow, having more dialogue and better solution for them, WHAT! There are many conflicts where, I don't want to fight them but it can't be avoided, somehow I just spared them and can let them go. "This is the best game ever!" took the word out of my mouth. To be fair, it's not every encounter does this, even there's many bosses where it feels anticlimatic because they can't be spared even though, yes, I know they're just pure evil, but having more dialogue or finisher would be much more fun.

This game is beautiful, beautiful places, beautiful city, beautiful design, but let's be real, 80% of the time I'm just looking at the ground and that's what I kind of hate in this game. I swear everytime I navigate the characters I want to cry because it's so difficult to navigate, and I have to navigate 4 people. Especially in the cities. It's really hard to navigate to each floor and sometimes I missclicked and starting the dialogue with my teammates like, "Okay Gale, move out of the way". And yes, you can make it horizontal angle, like a third person angle, but now it's harder to click. The dissapoinment is that when I tried to adjust it on options or googled it, they want me to instal mods and I really don't like that solution. So having more optimization on settings would be really great. I can't even do the third person angle in exploration because things like "ambushed" or "traps" are everywhere. That's why the dialogue are more fun to watch because they're in horizontal angle where I can see the skies or see the background, but not the floor.

I do love the characters in the game. I played as Wyll because he's giving a main character energy and I didn't customize my character, because and because, I thought he will talk in dialogue. These dialogues are so awkward because my character doesn't say the word I chose, making it more bland. Even worse on romance options, Shadowheart the love of my life, my character just smiling awkwardly not saying the love words and it feels one-way.  I do believe having more playable teammates are not a good approach especially in "companion quest". I love Jaheira, Astorion, Minsc, and Halsin quest, but they're not even in my main team. The worst part is I used them for that specific quest but not having gear on because I'm not even aware of their gameplay. I bet the quests are bland if they're not in the team, I was even in awe in Astorion performance and I don't even like his gameplay. It would be great if these characters are scattered in the whole map and meeting them as I explore the place or better yet, fighting alongside as NPC in the big fight, but they're just ended up in the camp talking like, "Yes we defeat them together", no you don't...

I had so much fun in my playthrough because the class and teammates roles are diverse enough where I made my teammates like Lae'zel, Shadowheart, and Gale being the most broken character ever wearing the most drippy gears meanwhile my Wyll are focusing on charisma, learning music (I go with the flute), and having all the essential skills. That is like peak roleplaying immersion gameplay wise. It does get a bit dissapointing where I maxed level so early in the late game and can't be overleveled, but I just have to go through the harder difficulty I guess.

Honestly, the game is really fun in terms of roleplaying, immersive world, fun and quality-over-quantity side-quest, loveable and memorable characters, varied builds, freedom of gameplay, but things like frustating navigation, okay main-story conclusion, looking at the ground gameplay, "solve things by downloading this mods", held me back to loving it more. 8,5/10

You already know this is a great game. I just want to nuance it a bit by highlighting a couple of things which annoyed me:
One is the "all doors should be open" approach to game design. You can romance pretty much every adult humanoid you spend time with (non-exclusive), and you can completely respec your character mid-adventure for a nominal fee. I get that some will see these as positives, but to me, it just cheapens it a bit, and dimishes the immersion.

Another issue is that there is a bit of fatigue towards the end. I found the earlier quests and stories more compelling than what's in the last third, where the game keeps throwing even more side quests at you, at the same time as the main story heads towards the standard "save the world" kind of end. Perhaps it's just that I've seen this so many times, the stakes always have to be raised to cataclysmic levels. Perhaps it's in part because this is a very large game, and they feel the stakes have to keep increasing throughout. Still, fact remains that I care more about what I did in the first two acts than the last.

Despite these complaints though, I absolutely recommend BG3. It's a fantastic game in most ways. It's deep and detailed, vast in content and possibilities, impressive in presentation.

Larian Studios has once again proven their mastery, taking it to new heights with Baldur’s Gate 3. The game delivers an excellent story, carefully structured across three acts, with Act 3 standing out as the clear highlight.

For explorers, this is a content-rich adventure—a true fun fest that can easily last 150+ hours if played comprehensively. The world is brimming with secrets, quests, and branching paths that reward curiosity at every turn.

Choices matter deeply here. Players can go down good, bad, or neutral paths, shaping their adventure to their liking. These decisions lead to game-altering moments that make every playthrough feel unique and personal.

Boss encounters are particularly impressive. Many are optional yet fully fleshed out, with proper leveling and unique story elements that add layers of depth to the narrative. This design choice makes every confrontation feel meaningful rather than filler.

Companions are another strength. Larian has crafted optional companions with strong story integration, ensuring that each one feels like a natural part of the journey rather than an afterthought. Their arcs intertwine beautifully with the main plot, enhancing immersion.

One of the most striking improvements over Divinity: Original Sin 2 is the use of cutscenes. They are a genuine game-changer, elevating the storytelling.

Overall, Baldur’s Gate 3 is a monumental achievement in role-playing games. With its rich narrative, expansive content, and groundbreaking presentation, it earns nothing less than a 10/10.

Dark, cold, empty. Gears grind all around. The pale light of crystals and mushrooms falls on the cracked roof of the Sorcerer's Tower. Mechanical arms embrace you, speaking words of care to someone who is no longer there. You find only fragments of her story: Lenora. She was lonely, loved theater and poetry, and had a pet. Her magical research remains untouched until you find it.
You're held in the cold, metallic embrace of a robot. Home seems unattainable, the journey endless, and the parasite within unstoppable. Suddenly, a warm hand.
- Soldier, are you all right? - A red-skinned girl with a broken horn and new scars looks at you. You nod. Behind you are your comrades: an elf vampire arguing with a mage, a cleric smiling at his faithful dog Scratch, a Gith reading ancient records while a naive warlock tries to talk to a robot.
You smile, inhale the stinking air of the Underdark, and clench your fists. A halberd-wielding companion taps you on the shoulder.
- Ready?
- Ready.
____________________________
For me, Baldur’s Gate 3 has become a personal outlet – a space for emotional release, creativity, and escape. It’s an elaborate world with a life of its own that invites you in, lets you shape your own story, and makes you feel like part of something both warm and terrifying at the same time. There are no right or wrong choices, you do what you think is right, how you want to direct the story, adapting to the random, sometimes unfavorable, dice values.

What makes Baldur’s Gate 3 so powerful and so personal is the sheer freedom it gives you. Built on the Dungeons & Dragons Fifth Edition system, the game offers a level of creativity in both combat and exploration that few RPGs even attempt. It’s not just about stats and turns – it’s about improvisation. Lose your weapon? Improvise with a nearby object or even toss a party member! Can’t reach that annoying archer? Drench them in magical darkness and force them out. Angered a genie? No problem – turn yourself into a delicious wheel of cheese and hope no one takes a bite. This kind of playful chaos makes the world feel truly alive and makes every decision, however absurd or heartfelt, yours.

I also want to highlight the amazing community and the genuine support from the developers. The game inspired an incredible amount of creativity from videos and fan art to cosplays and memes. The six years of titanic effort poured into making this game paid off not just financially, but in the deep love people feel for Larian Studios. Throughout development, they actively listened to player feedback, adjusted mechanics, fixed bugs, and reworked entire systems based on what the community needed. Even after release, they didn’t stop adding features like multiplayer and official mod support, which lets players enhance the game with everything from subtle cosmetic tweaks to brand-new locations you can explore with your companions or real-life friends. They’ve also continued to release major patches, expand origin character content, improve endings, and polish narrative details based on fan input. Their dedication didn’t end on launch day; they treated the game as a living world, and the players as part of its ongoing evolution.

When it comes to mechanics, Baldur’s Gate 3 excels in every aspect, from combat to dialogue and puzzles. Built on the foundation of D&D Fifth Edition, the game implements the famous d20 dice rolls, bringing that classic sense of uncertainty and excitement to every action – whether it’s attacking in combat, convincing someone in a tense conversation, or searching for hidden chests. The puzzles in the game are another highlight, often requiring you to think creatively or use your surroundings to your advantage. It’s not all about brute force. Sometimes it’s about using your wits, whether you're figuring out ancient riddles in Shar’s Temple, cracking open secret doors in an old vampire castle, or navigating moral dilemmas in Druid Grove. This balance of tactics, cleverness, and roleplay makes the world feel immersive and dynamic.

You'll want to play Baldur's Gate 3 over and over again, as each new playthrough reveals unexpected aspects of the story and characters. Thanks to a huge number of options for how events unfold, a choice of classes, races, and decisions, as well as different endings. Each time, the story unfolds in a new way, and your actions affect the world and the fate of your companions. Even after hundreds of hours, you will still find new quests, dialogues, and unexpected consequences of your actions, making replay not only possible, but exciting.

Baldur's Gate 3 lore and locations are breathtaking in their scope and depth, as the game is set in the legendary Forgotten Realms, one of the most elaborate worlds in D&D. The story leads the player through the most diverse corners of the Sword Coast: from the Emerald grove of druids and the magical darkness of Moonrise Towers to the gloomy dungeons of the Underworld and the majestic city of Baldur's Gate, one of the largest and most influential cities of Faerûn. Each location is filled with a unique atmosphere, myths and stories, and the world is home to representatives of many races and factions: humans, elves, dwarves, dwarves, tieflings, dwarves, orcs and even dragons.

If you’ve ever wanted a game that respects your choices, challenges your mind, and speaks to your heart this is the one. Baldur’s Gate 3 isn’t just a triumph of storytelling and design; it’s also a perfect introduction to the world of Dungeons & Dragons. You don’t need to know the rules or have dice on your shelf. This game teaches you through play, and by the time you realize it, you’re already thinking like a true adventurer. Whether you’re a long-time fan of RPGs or someone taking their first step into this kind of world, this game welcomes you in and doesn’t let go.

The game is fun. It has really awesome mechanics and the setting is such an atmospheric masterpiece. It has a TON of flaws in its current state though. The major glaring issue that aggravates me the most is the unfair damage spikes that occur.
 I have a character that is "near" invincible. I consistently run juiced t16 way stones fully corrupted with ZERO issues. However, you will begin to consistently experience a wonderful thing. You get one shotted by a monster from off screen or something exploding that you literally cannot see. No way to avoid, no way to prepare. You're just running happily, full health full shield, and BOOM, dead. And upon that, their xp loss penalty for dying is completely ridiculous. Good luck getting past lvl 90. You die unfairly on a map, you loose 10% of your total xp needed to get the next level. Why GGG thought this was a good idea is beyond me. 
Also, if you die on a certain map, even playing it was pointless because you cannot repeat the map with the same benefits again, or even use your modifiers as a punishment for dying. I get that GGG wants to have a difficult experience but this is just brutal and honestly, not fun when it happens constantly. 
The economy is broken as well, with players taking advantage of the market to the point where realistically working towards a top tear build becomes impossible unless you can play/grind for 8 hours a day. Its almost like this current state is only geared towards streamers and content creators that can play this game for their living. Issues like these create issues with "currency" sellers being a source for people to pay real money for currency to use to get the exact gear needed to be viable. 
 I think they have something special here, but at this current time, I cannot recommend jumping into it until they change some of these things. And this is from someone who has played about 500 hours. Wait until its fully released. I will edit and update this review as changed come across that effect the game positively

After 116 hours in Path of Exile 2, I can confidently say it has completely hooked me. I started as an Invoker Monk running a Herald of Thunder build, and the combat never gets old—watching the entire screen erupt in lightning while mobs explode before they can even reach my character is incredibly satisfying. The visual feedback, sound design, and pacing of combat make every encounter feel powerful and rewarding.

Even after investing so many hours into my main character, I still find myself excited to log in because there’s always something new to experiment with. I’ve already started leveling a Mercenary and a Sorceress alt, and each class feels distinct enough to keep the experience fresh rather than repetitive.

I didn’t play the first Path of Exile, but I’ve spent plenty of time in Diablo 3 and Diablo 4, and what stands out here is the depth of builds and the sense of long-term progression. There’s a real feeling that your character is evolving into something uniquely yours, especially once your build starts to fully “come online.”

If you enjoy action RPGs with deep customization, impactful combat, and builds that can completely transform how the game feels, Path of Exile 2 is absolutely worth diving into. Even 100+ hours in, it still feels like I’m just getting started.

I'm giving this game a positive review, but at the moment I can't keep playing this game because it's too frustrating.

Let's start with the positives. 

The graphics look amazing, I use DLSS with Preset M and it looks fantastic and performs well. However, when I started playing I would get crashes randomly, but I found out it was because of the audio. If you turn the audio quality down to lowest, 95% of the crashes go away and you can actually play the game. I maybe have had 1 crash in a week of play.

The campaign is fun as hell. My only gripe is that you have to hit every nook and cranny of every mission/map to make sure you don't miss anything during the campaign, it can be tedious, but it wasn't terrible. I love the skills and gems, equipment drops are great, trading currency for equipment in the in game marketplace is super easy and wonderful, and a step up from Poe 1.

Now as to why I can't keep playing this game...
The end game is an absolute mess.... When you get to high level Mapping, you are constantly 1 shot in unfair ways, and this takes away exp from your character, losing hours of playtime towards that characters end game level up. Even stacking armor, ES and resistances, you will still get unfairly 1 tapped, out of nowhere, hit reg will be off, you dodged the attack but it still hit you, your character got stuck on a pebble, there's too much clutter on screen to even be able to see what hit you, etc. And if you stack defense, then you lose offense, making it take significantly longer to clear maps, but if you stack defense, you still get 1 tapped. So you might as well run as a glass cannon and dodge at everything to clear it quicker, this makes the game really just a game of chance instead of what they were initially going for which was a combination of character, gear and skill.

The trials of Chaos endgame is another failure. The stacking debuffs are not fun, you are continually 1 tapped, and it becomes a chore to do anything in the end game rather than a fun grind and challenge. Maybe I will come back and level up other characters just for fun, but right now I'm taking a break. I really wanted to enjoy the end game, but it's just unbalanced, not fun and wasting time that I could be using to have fun doing something else.

Path of Exile 2 refines and expands its predecessor’s deep systems into a more cohesive, responsive, and mechanically expressive ARPG, blending familiar loot-driven progression with ambitious combat, skill, and scaling mechanics.

⚔️ Combat & Skill System — Fluid At Its Core

Combat in PoE2 feels sharper and more impactful than before. Hits connect with a satisfying weight, movement is snappy, and evasion/dodge feels like an active choice rather than a passive stat. The combat loop — move, position, attack, react — has more rhythmic responsiveness, making both clearing hordes and fighting bosses feel mechanical rather than random.

Skill customization remains a defining system, but in PoE2 it’s been streamlined without losing depth. Skills aren’t tied to a simple gem-socket system; they are now part of a hybrid action framework that blends traditional ARPG inputs with modular modifiers. Each ability has:

Clear roles (burst, sustain, crowd control),

Scalable augmentations (AoE radius, cast speed, additional effects),

And modifiers you slot in that behave predictably instead of randomly.

This makes builds feel like intentional constructions of mechanics, not just collections of numbers.

🌳 Passive & Specialization Trees — Strategic Expression

The passive tree has been reworked to be more meaningful and less sprawling, focusing on distinct paths of mechanical identity rather than just raw stat increases. You still invest progression points, but choices now yield clear gameplay changes — whether that’s stronger elemental conversion, improved dodge windows, or enhanced life leech synergy. There’s less “grind for incremental numbers” and more decisions that change how your build plays.

Each class’s specialization isn’t a dead end — rather, it unlocks unique mechanical layers that shape combat rhythm and role:

Frontliners gain better positioning and threat management tools,

Spellcasters get stronger charge and area mechanics,

Rangers enhance mobility and reactive systems.

Classes feel mechanically distinct, not just cosmetically.

🪙 Loot & Crafting — Predictable Power Growth

PoE2 keeps its signature loot depth but retools item crafting to be less opaque and more strategic. Currency items are tied to specific upgrade outcomes rather than random rerolls, giving players clearer control over gear growth. This turns crafting into a tactical system rather than a gamble:

Want more sockets? You know which currency to use.

Want to tailor resistances or utility mods? You can focus your resources mechanically.

This removes a lot of the old uncertainty and elevates player intention in gear progression.

🧠 Difficulty Scaling & Encounter Design

Difficulty ramps through predictable but challenging encounters — enemy behaviors telegraph more clearly, and mechanics reward observation and reaction rather than blind DPS stacking. Boss fights especially feel like mechanical puzzles in motion: pattern recognition, positioning, and resource timing matter just as much as stats.

Encounters aren’t random spawns — they are designed with mechanical intent, meaning teamwork (in co-op) and build synergy feel meaningful rather than incidental.

🗺️ Endgame & World Systems

The endgame here is no longer “reach a level cap and hope for better RNG” — the Atlas and region progression systems are player-driven loops. You choose how to scale challenges, manipulate map modifiers, and decide which mechanics you want to emphasize:

Higher risk for higher reward?

Targeted boss tracking?

Layered modifiers that dramatically change combat?

These decisions shape how the world responds to you, and that adaptive mechanical feedback is the backbone of long-term engagement.

10/10 — refined combat systems, intentional gear mechanics, and strategic progression loops that reward both tactical play and build creativity.

Path of Exile 2 has been a really pleasant surprise for me. The biggest selling point was native local co-op with shared screen on PC. Unlike Diablo IV, Grim Dawn, Titan Quest, Torchlight and even the first Path of Exile, which only offer online co-op and/or couch co-op on consoles, this lets me play on the same PC with my wife. That's a huge selling point for us, and I honestly think the store page should clearly mention it with the appropriate tag.

I barely played the original PoE, so I cannot really comment on lore or continuity. I have just reached Act 3, so I have no feedback on the endgame content yet, which seems to be the focus of many controversial reviews. So far I am just enjoying the strong Diablo 2 vibes. I played that game nonstop back in the day and loved its atmosphere, and the environments here feel very close in spirit.

The graphics are good, with a strong art style, and performance has been solid for an Early Access title. I do not have deep experience with classes, but the three I tried felt balanced and different enough to support distinct gameplay flows.

Some quality of life improvements are needed, especially for the gamepad interface. I would love easier access to certain features across menus, like being able to socket support gems directly from the skill menu, and generally making some interactions less convoluted. That said, it is still Early Access, so this feels understandable.

I did run into some server instability, heavy lag, and a few cases where the game froze with a "Game Paused" message. From what I read around this may be tied to ping going over 100 ms. That could be a problem if you live far from the available servers, so it might be smart to check the server list before buying the Early Access support pack. I also had long freezes after several hours of play that eventually turned into a loading screen and put me back exactly where I left off, with no progress loss. I am not sure if that is a local memory issue or a server desync.

Overall, my experience has been positive. As a Diablo 2 LoD veteran playing alongside my partner, who is still fairly new to isometric ARPGs, we are both having a great time.

This is my reflection on what I have played, nothing more nothing less.

Path of Exile 2 Early Access. Overall, I like the game — it has strong ideas and is genuinely addictive. Progression feels satisfying, and if you can invest the time, the endgame is reachable for normal players.

Campaign: Being able to skip the campaign would be a welcome quality of life option. Running it repeatedly gets boring no matter how fast you are.

Classes: The Druid is a great addition. There are some rough edges, but overall, it’s fun and well designed.

Temple: I don’t enjoy the Temple runs. The RNG required to create a viable run is frustrating, and I don’t find it fun to repeat it many times until I get the setup I want. And in that, atlas mechanics work better and faster, so temples do not make sense for a player like me.

Technical: The game is not very stable on PC. I experience a lot of rubber banding, and the Nvidia driver issue should have been resolved ASAP. Stability and server reliability need to be top priorities; I have died dozens of times because the server is not performing.

Mid season balance changes: As a casual player, mid season nerfs are a dealbreaker. If I invest limited time into a build to reach endgame and it gets hit with a 25% damage penalty, I’m unlikely to come back. I understand rebalancing between seasons but changing a build mid season after players have committed to it is extremely frustrating.

Verdict: An okay Early Access overall, with good core design and addictive progression, but stability, server issues, and mid season nerfs are the main problems for me.

Closing
This isn’t a bad game, it’s an Early Access with the wrong priorities right now. If you’re a casual player who values your time, wait for launch or for the devs to fix stability and rethink mid season balance decisions.

The game is polished, slower, and heavily curated. Progression is padded, power is drip-fed, and player experimentation is tightly constrained. Where PoE1 rewarded knowledge, creativity, and breaking systems, PoE2 rewards patience and repetition. It’s less about discovering powerful interactions and more about enduring the grind.
Combat looks good but limits agency, and many systems feel designed to maximize playtime rather than depth. Cosmetics lean toward safe reskins instead of meaningful identity, reinforcing the sense that the game values retention metrics over player expression.
The developers are clearly skilled, but their design priorities are misaligned with what made Path of Exile special. If this were a new IP, it would be fine. As a sequel, it’s a step backward.
Verdict: Polished, conservative, and soulless. Until it re-embraces player-driven chaos and real build freedom, this is a thumbs down for PoE1 veterans.

TL;DR – Diablo tragic, full-time husband with 2 kids and 14 wives, still enjoying the game.

As above, I’m a Diablo tragic. I won’t defend it or pretend it’s something it’s not — but I’ll also complain about it while being 11 seasons deep with 5,000+ hours played.

I never played PoE1. I always assumed it was inaccessible and just “not for me”.

I picked up PoE 2 a few weeks ago expecting to play maybe 20 hours and say “yeah nah”. I can’t lie — I’m 61 hours in, still have no idea what I’m doing, but I’ve reached early endgame and I’m actually enjoying the mapping system (felt a lot like LE).

Building a character is nothing like any Diablo game, which has been a steep learning curve. I still have zero idea how crafting really works, but one of the biggest things I’ve noticed is the community. It’s way more active and easily 1000% more helpful. I know 60 hours isn’t much, but I haven’t had a single bad interaction yet.

The game itself has a steep learning curve — you can’t just face-tank everything — but it’s not “souls-like”. The campaign is fun, but I’ll be honest: I’m not keen to do it again.

Game: 9/10
Story: N/A
Fun: 8/10
Accessibility: 8/10

Compared to D4? At this stage, unless the Diablo team pulls something wild for Season 12+, I’ll be over here.

If you’re a dad/husband/mum/wife working 12+ hour days with kids and think this game isn’t for you — think again and give it a go. On a good week, I might get 10–15 hours total, and I’m still enjoying this far more than D4.

Will update as time goes on.

Honestly, I don't get the hype for this game. I'm coming from 200+ hours in Diablo Immortal and Diablo 4 Season 3, so I know what I'm talking about when it comes to quality ARPGs. Path of Exile 2 feels like a massive step backward for the genre.

Here are the negatives (because I couldn't find any positives):

Way too slow and Clunky: The character moves like they have constant lag. In Diablo 4, combat is fluid and visceral; here, you're locked into animations forever. They tried to copy Elden Ring with the dodge roll but failed miserably. If I wanted to play a Souls-like, I'd play one, not this.

The Passive Tree is a JOKE: Who has time to read all that? It's just artificial complexity to make "tryhards" feel smart. They should simplify it like D4 where you have a clear path. Having to use an external guide just to play is bad game design, period.

No Auto-Pathing? It's 2026, where is the button to auto-walk to the quest objective? I got lost in the first map for like 10 minutes. Mobile games solved this years ago.

Dark and generic graphics: Everything is just gray and brown. It lacks the art direction and polish of Blizzard games. You can tell it's an ancient engine with some HD textures slapped on top.

Archaic Flask System: Why do I have to kill monsters to refill potions? They should just have a cooldown or be infinite. Outdated mechanic from the 90s.

Conclusion: A pretentious game made for people with no jobs and no social life who enjoy suffering. If you want a real ARPG, just buy the Diablo expansion. Hopefully, they add a Battle Pass in the future so I can pay to skip levels and bypass this boring campaign, but knowing these "stingy" devs, they probably won't.

[b]Path of Exile 2 has the potential to become one of the best action RPGs ever — but right now, in early access, I do not recommend buying it.[/b]

I’ve played PoE 2 for over [b]1,000 hours[/b] in its first year of early access, and I don’t regret the time — but the experience has been increasingly frustrating, and in its current state I don’t think it’s a fair or stable experience for new players.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Economy Is Not Optional[/h2]

PoE 2 is a game that — in my experience — can only be enjoyed properly if you meaningfully participate in the in-game economy. To do that effectively you need premium stash tabs and especially AFK shop tabs. Without them, trading efficiently is difficult, risky, prone to scam attempts, and time-consuming.

Community creator GhazzyTV once described Path of Exile as:

[quote]
“Free to try, not free to play.”
[/quote]

That still applies to PoE 2.  
Meaningful economy participation costs additional money.
Plus, PoE 2 early access costs money straight away! It will only be [i]"free to play"[/i] on full release.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Fate of the Vaal – Economy Collapse[/h2]

The most recent Fate of the Vaal league exposed how fragile the economy can be. A new league mechanic — the Temple — was poorly balanced at release, and an abrupt rewards increase just before a holiday break caused massive inflation. By the time GGG returned and patched the situation, many players were so far behind they could no longer participate meaningfully. A league intended to last ~4 months became effectively unplayable after about [b]1 month[/b] for a large portion of the player base.

GGG did not:

[list]
[*] Roll out a patch quickly  
[*] Reset the economy  
[*] Roll back progress  
[*] Punish exploiters  
[/list]

The situation was justified with “it’s early access.”

Technically true. Practically devastating.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Community Response Says Everything[/h2]

The community organized and crowdfunded a private league called:

[b]Second Wind: Fate of the Vaal[/b]

[list]
[*] ~51,000 total slots  
[*] ~48,000 registered players  
[*] One of the largest private leagues in PoE history  
[/list]

Tens of thousands of players voluntarily paid to join a community-run reset league because they wanted:

[list]
[*] A fresh economy  
[*] A fair start  
[*] A playable league  
[/list]

That level of participation speaks louder than any forum post.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]There Are Good Things[/h2]

To be clear:

[list]
[*] Combat feels good and challenging  
[*] Build depth is promising  
[*] Core systems have real potential  
[/list]

But none of that matters when:

[list]
[*] The economy can collapse without proper measures taken by GGG
[*] Exploiters go unpunished and are incentivized to always look for new opportunities to break the game for everyone
[*] Progress becomes meaningless due to developer negligence  
[*] Player time investment isn’t protected  
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Verdict[/h2]

I believe PoE 2 can become something special, maybe even the best action RPG so far.

[b]But right now: I do not recommend buying Path of Exile 2 during early access.[/b]

Wait for later development stages when economy handling, balance processes, and player-time protection are clearly more mature.

I expect — and hope — to change this review in the future.

COULDN'T GET INTO POE1?  READ ON:

I booked no more than 10 hours in Path of Exile across a couple season attempts.  The biggest issue isn't even that I found it daunting or intimidating - I just thought it didn't feel good to play.  The camera hanged unimaginably close to your character's head.  Click-to-move didn't bring me joy in the accessibility age.  Very few tooltips and progression recommendations made for a confusing experience where I could not determine if I was effective, or how to become such.  

I'm 286 hours into PoE 2 at time of writing, most of this time spanning across 3 characters in both Solo Self Found and Trade leagues.  The SINGLE criticism I can drum up across nigh 300 hours would be aimed specifically at the league structures:  SSF can feel a little slow and sometimes punishing since loot and currencies drop slower as one person without an economy; conversely, trade league felt almost too "easy" for me as you could acquire high-grade gear and currency with very little effort or luck.  I still haven't decided if I will main a specific league, or which one I would main.  

To be at almost 300 hours into the game and still feel like I'm in the "experimentation" phase of feeling out a character, the progression and gear systems, the league's nuances and interactivity...just feels like such a joy and a blessing.  By this much time I'm usually done and dusted with most of my library picks, and I'm staring at this title (still in Early Access for probably another 3 quarters, BTW) and just cannot imagine when I will stop having fun.  There's SO MANY characters I want to build on my own and take through the campaign and try endgame progression with.

As a player who likes very minimal engagement with guides and meta playstyles, I have not felt ineffective with the exception of brief slumps where the build or my gear need an adjustment.  At my own humble devices, I devised a build that took me to the 90s in SSF and it still has room to become much stronger.  I have reached a point where I can see the benefit of trade league - knowing it might take several hours to grind some currencies or loot when I could just start hawking my own items and quickly buy upgrades.  The crazy part is that if you don't like SSF, you can just switch - for the most part mitigating half of my grievances.  

Bringing it all around, if you don't want to play the economy, you don't have to.  If you don't want to play alone, you don't have to.  If you don't want you use a guide, you don't have to.  

IF YOU DON'T WANT TO PLAY THIS GAME BECAUSE YOU DIDN'T LIKE POE 1, PLEASE RECONSIDER!

Dead by Daylight is a great game — but only if you enjoy diverse and sometimes unpredictable gameplay.

For Survivors
There will be matches where the killer is far more experienced than you, and others where the killer barely knows how to use their abilities. It’s important to remember that this is a team-based game. You depend on your teammates, and they depend on you.

From time to time, you’ll encounter players who don’t cooperate, beginners who are still learning, or even people who are trolling. However, there are also moments when teamwork feels perfectly coordinated — even without voice communication. Solo queue can be very challenging, even for skilled players, so I highly recommend playing with friends or with reliable teammates you meet in the game.

Most importantly, you need to maintain a “this is just a game” mindset. You will die often — sometimes a lot — and many times it won’t even be your fault.

For Killers
In my opinion, playing killer can feel more challenging because it’s a 1v4 situation. You have to focus on many things at once. You must learn to use your power effectively while keeping track of generators and survivor movements. Decision-making is crucial: knowing when to end a chase, when to pressure generators, and how to manage map control can determine the outcome of the match.

Playing killer can also be frustrating. Survivors may stun or blind you repeatedly, or they may play in highly coordinated groups. However, just like with survivor gameplay, the key is maintaining a healthy mindset and remembering that it’s just a game.

Overall
Both survivor and killer roles are difficult in their own ways. Some players will disagree and argue that one side is easier or that the game is unfair. In my opinion, those players either need more practice or should consider whether this game suits them.

One more important point: this game is not pay-to-win. I’ve often seen people claim that it is, but owning premium characters does not guarantee success. I’ve seen both strong and weak players using paid characters. Losing to someone who owns premium content doesn’t automatically mean they had an unfair advantage. I would rate Dead by Daylight an 8–8.5/10.

Thank you for reading my review! If you enjoyed it and think it deserves recognition, I would truly appreciate a Community Award — but only if you feel it’s earned.

I booted up Battlefield 6 expecting chaos.
I got chaos.
But like… the cinematic, “my squad just accidentally leveled an entire shopping mall” kind of chaos.

First of all, this game understands that sometimes you don’t want to be a soldier. Sometimes you want to be a mildly trained tornado with a rifle. And BF6 says, “Absolutely. Here’s a tank, a helicopter, and a building that used to exist.”

The destruction is back and it’s personal. Walls? Optional. Cover? Temporary. That sniper who’s been camping for 12 minutes? Congratulations, he now lives outside because the building doesn’t.

Gunplay feels chunky in the best way. Every weapon sounds like it was recorded by someone aggressively slamming car doors in a thunderstorm. Recoil feels real enough that I look tactical, but forgiving enough that my panic spraying occasionally counts as “suppressing fire.”

Vehicles? Absolute menace. I spawned, blinked, and suddenly I was in a jet I absolutely did not know how to fly. Did I survive? No. Did I look cool for three seconds? Also no. But I tried, and that’s what matters.

The real magic though? Battlefield moments™.

Random medic revives you while bullets are flying everywhere.

Entire squad charges through smoke like we rehearsed it (we did not).

That one engineer who exists solely to ruin every vehicle’s day.

Pros:

Destruction that solves camping problems permanently

Huge maps that make every match feel like a war movie

Vehicles that let me roleplay as “professional accident”

Squad plays that make you feel like tactical geniuses

Cons:

I still cannot land helicopters

My K/D ratio is a suggestion

Overall: 10/10 would accidentally redeploy my entire squad into a burning crater again.

If you like big maps, loud explosions, and turning “strategic objective” into “historical landmark that used to be here,” Battlefield 6 delivers.

The game is good. I built a PC and bought it because I played BF4 when I was a teenager and I've missed every Battlefield since then. I really wanted to play each of them. And I finally got my hands on BF6, and it feels great to be back, personally as someone whose best weapon was the M98B, I like the sniping, I like getting to experience the sweet spot mechanic from BF1, the fluid crawling from BFV.
In BF4, we used to say: "PTFO". And unless I'm playing Rush, it seems like the playerbase has turned away from that motive. When I play engineer, no vehicles are getting painted. When I play recon, none of the painted vehicles are getting hit. It has become a giant game of Team Deathmatch, same goes for the Gauntlet. I think priorities have changed, people desire more intensity, more dopamine, less need for patience, and they're getting that with smaller maps, faster close range TTK. Holding the objective has become perceived as camping.
BUT, I have no idea what people talk about when talking about disastrous maps or bad hit registration or sniping AAs. The pilots and tankers in my games live for very long, to the point where I need to switch to engineer and die to them many times before I get one shot off at them and deal 650 damage when their flares are down, only for them to tuck behind a hill and restock. My bullets seem to hit just fine and I'd argue that my hit registration in Valorant is worse than in BF6. Maps are fine. I do not see myself wanting a 20x scope again, the bullet travel time starts getting troublesome already on maps like Blackwell fields or Mirak Valley. I've seen the record shots of 2km plus on Firestorm, and I don't desire those kills. There isn't a range point bonus, and aggressive recon has always seemed as a better way to play than sniping from a hill. Again, PTFO, my score per minute with M98B was abominable. Speaking of Blackwell Fields, I get that people don't like that map. I, for one, love it. The hills have good blind spots to hide in from the snipers and tanks. There are 5 man squad vehicles to provide transport to objectives as well as a mobile spawn point that's somewhat protected from tanks. Unless AA is LITERALLY sniping from its spawn, it is at risk of getting taken down by engineers and tanks as soon as it crests the first hill. If my memory serves me well, I've almost never seen AA far away from spawn in BF4 either.
My only complaint about this game is the progression. I saw that there is XP tweaking incoming, but right now, I only have one weapon at level 50, and with how thermal 6x scopes or suppressors or synthetic tips are unlocked at level 35+, and there being 3 camo unlocks per weapon, I don't want the 500 kill masteries back. And then yet again, the way I'd do those in BF4? I'd grind Rush or Domination or Metro or Operation Locker until I had the mastery, and only then I'd use the fully customized weapon in Conquest. Unlocking the suppressor and bipod for a gun often required me to get 100 kills with it first, excluding battlepacks. I had to run the SAR-21 with the same muzzle break and red dot combo for 80 kills. And I wasn't good with recoil, now i at least get progress for kill participation and getting kills at objectives.

I could likely write a book on my thoughts on BF6, but I'll likely keep this brief as most of the issues have been written about ad-nauseum at this point.

Like most other veteran battlefield players (I've been playing since BF2), I was extremely excited seeing gameplay trailers for 6 because it seemed like DICE (what was left of it anyway) was finally listening to it's players, and we were finally getting back to what makes Battlefield feel distinctly different from other shooters on the market. How wrong we all were. 

During the beta, there was a big sentiment in the community that the game perhaps was feeling more like a mix of BF and CoD than BF itself. Now, i will say that I didn't really mind this, if it was a way to pull some players away from CoD while still trying to keep BF players happy, so be it. I'm willing to compromise on certain things that other hardcore vets of the series very clearly were not. The beta showed off only small maps with 1 larger map being liberation peak. The problem was Liberation Peak is terribly designed and produces some of the most one-sided games you'll play. The other maps were small and just didn't feel properly balanced vehicle wise and were just way too fast paced with a the TTK of guns being so low it felt more like you were in a meat grinder of just spawning and dying constantly. Overall, it felt like the bones were there, but something was just off about the gameplay itself.

Come launch time, really not much had changed from the Beta. It was hard to understand that all the feedback basically was ignored. I personally did not really care. I played A LOT of this game in a pretty short amount of time. However, a lot of the common Battlefield issues showed their head. Netcode was horrendous (this has been marginally improved at least). The TTK is still far far too low, it just feels like you die so fast that for a battlefield game it makes your typical strategies/squad based play tough. SMG's for so long have been absolute laser beams, and honestly most guns feel like laser beams. Burst firing is not really needed after you unlock certain attachments for guns. Speaking of attachments, the unlock time/system for this game is absolutely horrendous. It takes SO LONG to unlock the attachments needed for guns it's unreal. They claim as of this review that's being looked at for season 2 and changed so we'll see.

We get to season 2 and there's just hardly any content in a 3 month timespan, which honestly, would not be as big of a deal if the current maps available were actually fun to play. Most of them are terrible, too fast paced, and just don't feel like Battlefield. DICE and EA have never understood that CoD players are not going to play their games long term. Your core audience wants Battlefield. If you don't deliver on that, they will simply not play it and then you have neither audience captured. 

I want to make clear that I actually enjoyed most of my time playing the game, it just got exhausting to play. There's simply too much going on all around you at all times, there's no time to breathe on almost any map. You're being shot at from so many angles with a TTK so low you barely have time to respond. The netcode is still an issue, the gun balance is still an issue, and in my opinion, it's simply too late to reverse course. 

My advice? Go find something else to play. The issue of course if you're like me, there really isn't many modern military shooters to play anymore. I thought this was going to be my game to play for years. I and most of us were so very wrong.

I am a huge BF fan and have been since BF3. I stopped playing after BF1 and never played BFV or BF2042. I was super excited to see BF6 was going to go back to it's roots and give players a modern setting again. The beta was really fun and imo showed the games potential, albeit with a lot of problems that you could chock up as 'beta issues' that you would think would be fixed when the game launched. However, as the honeymoon phase of BF6 has worn off, this game has so many issues that have yet to addressed. 

First off, it just feels bad to play. I think that might just be my opinion but the gunplay and movement to me just feels off. I really cant even explain it very well either. Something about the inconsistency between everything just makes it feel off. Sometimes you move around very easily and don't have any issues, the next you're getting stuck on a corner or ledge that you now have to mantle over. Sometimes your gun feels like you're a god and lasers people from across the map in seconds, and then right after feels like your barrel is a noodle and rounds hit everything but the target. 

Secondly, the maps are absolutely garbage. There are zero maps that I am excited to play on. None. In fact, I go to the filter settings and turn off several of them just to make sure I don't play on them. They are all way too small and every map feels like a meat grinder CoD match, even in Conquest. I understand the giant maps are slow and sometimes it may take some running to get into the action but that is part of BF. Not every scenario needs to throw you right into the action 24/7, there needs to be some time to breath. 

Thirdly, the monetization and cosmetics are annoying. No surprise that a triple A game has annoying microtransactions. It's an even harder pill to swallow when the cosmetics are just downright terrible. Pax Armata has the ugliest uniforms ever with their neon yellow/green colors and honestly all of the women in LMG/medic roles for the NATO side just feels forced and dumb. NATO does however have the better cosmetics. 

Fourthly, it feels like this game is just dead already and everything is so absurdly grindy. It takes forever to level up guns and unlock things to the point where you're probably going to be using the same meta gun over and over until you unlock the attachments you want for it and by that point you're just bored out of your mind playing the same 3 maps over and over using the same gun over and over.  

With season 2 finally around the corner, you would think that EA would try and fix some of these issues but instead they're just going to drip feed content and milk every penny they can with battlepasses and cosmetic bundles. Also, REDSEC is terrible and takes too many resources away from the multiplayer getting better. Battle royales are dead and should stop being implemented into every single new game coming out.

I'm torn whether I should make a + or - review, but I think it's gotta be negative.
BF6 is mostly very enjoyable, but has a few major issues that really ruin the game for me.

TLDR: Botched classes, bad pacing and maps, lack of persistent servers and browser, bad live service, tedious progression, but some great new features. Still might be fixable in the future.


Lets start with core gameplay issues.

- The Class system. BF3 and BF4 mediocre class balance, but DICE revised classes in BF1 and BF5 into a system where each class feels very useful and is well defined. Each class fits their role because of their gadgets AND weapons. But, all that refining of the classes in BF1/V was thrown out in BF6, and now they've basically gone back to mediocre BF3/4 class balancing. Class roles are now less defined because anyone can use any weapon at any time.
For example: They moved the spawn beacon from Recon to Assault. Honestly not a bad change if you think about it. Makes sure spawn beacons are used more aggressively on the frontlines instead of camping in the back of the map. Except, wait a minute. An assault class can equip a sniper rifle due to open weapons so now DICE has basically just made a more powerful Recon class by giving it grenade launchers too. This isn't the end of the world, but why a step back?

-My next issue is the pacing of the game. There is simply no downtime or time to breathe in this game due to  intentional design. All the maps feel optimized so that you run in to fights around every corner or two. Part of the issue is that you auto heal, and heal from medic bags and pouches insanely fast. In previous games when someone takes damage, they're stuck holding a building for a while slowing down the entire match. In BF6 you auto heal back to full health in 10 seconds, if you have a medic bag nearby it's 5 seconds. In previous games a medic bag heals you in 10 seconds and auto heal takes 20-30. Remember in previous games how you could poke someone for half health and push and finish them off while they regen behind cover? That doesn't happen in this game because while you push them they've already healed and then they peek and kill you in the open. There might be too much reviving lol.

- The small average map size also adds to the pacing issue. Every map in this game is way too small. The average BF6 map feels smaller than Argonne Forest, Suez, Devastation, Aerodrome, Flood Zone, Propaganda and feel like the following small maps from older games: Al Marj Encampment, Fort De Vaux, and Operation Locker.
Out of the 11 maps in the game right now, there are only 4 that have jets, and 2 of them barely feel big enough for jets. Season 2 brings 2 new maps and neither supports jets. Only 1 supports helicopters.
The lack of variety is what makes me burn out on this game so quickly. There are like 2 truly large scale "Battlefield" Maps. Mirak Valley and Operation Firestorm. Mirak Valley is by far the best map in the game, but compared to any BF4, 1, or V map its so average. Playing Mirak Valley Conquest or Escalation is actually very fun most of the time. But it's like one of 2 or 3 maps that play like traditional large scale BF, and so I almost exclusively play those and get burnt out quickly and quit playing.
I love BF for its variety in gameplay. I love playing large scale vehicle maps, I also love playing my meatgrinder maps like Operation Underground from time to time and everything in between. But this game just has way too many meat grinder Tank and infantry only maps. I play BF for its sandbox. This game doesn't allow a whole lot of that. Most maps are corridors and alleys instead of battlefields.

- The lack of a server browser, but more importantly persistent servers is a massive issue. Everyone keeps talking about the missing server browser but a server browser is near useless without persistent servers. I don't even know how to hammer this into DICEs brain more than it already has been.
Every single time I've played Battlefield 3, Battlefield 4, Battlefield 1, and Battlefield 5 I have used the server browser to join a persistent server. Do not remove these features. 
I do not want to matchmake every 20 minutes. I'm already in a server with 63 other people, why split us all up and matchmake us again? Just to make me sit on the waiting for players screen or to fill my match up with bots? I don't care if it costs more money for a more permanent server. Have servers spin down like they did in BFV if there are too little players in them. Save money that way. Save money, but not at the cost of the product.

- Progression is way too long and tedious. Weapons take way too many kills to progress. It takes about 2000 kills per gun to fully level a weapon up and unlock all attachments. Someone crunched the numbers and it would take like 3000+ hours to level up all weapons. Gadgets can be a hassle to unlock due to the quite specific challenges. 

Live Service Issues:
- I used to despise live service games, but a few great ones like Helldivers 2, The Finals, and Arc Raiders have proven that they can be done very well. Battlefield has done the opposite of those 3 games. DICE has fumbled 4 live service games. SWBF2, BFV, BF2042, and BF6. 
If you compare the content you used to get out of DLCs in BF3, BF4, and BF1, to the live service content of BFV, BF2042, BF6, and SWBF2, it's laughable. BF4 did 23 post launch maps, and BF1 and 3 did 20. On the other hand BF5 did 11 post launch maps, BF2042 did 8, and BF6 is on track to do 8 over the course of 4 seasons or 1 year. 
There are also only like 3-4 guns per season instead of 6-10 per DLC like in previous games. On top of that there are no map variations and no weather conditions for any of these maps to make each match feel a little more unique which brings me to my next point.

Dice has taken map variations and game modes from previous games and turned them into limited time modes. The only map variation "currently" in the game is a snowy version of Manhattan. Well, actually it's not currently in the game because it was a limited time mode for Christmas. You can't play it anymore.
In season 2 DICE plans to add night variations to certain maps as more Limited Time Modes. If that wasn't bad enough they're bringing back the Operations game mode from BF1/V except IT'S A LIMITED TIME MODE. 

Yes, I want to play these modes so I'll come try them while they're limited, but then stop playing because they're no longer available. WHY NOT JUST MAKE THESE MAP VARIATIONS ALWAYS AVAILABLE SO THAT IT ADDS PERMANANT, NOT LIMITED, VALUE TO YOUR GAME AND I KEEP COMING BACK TO PLAY INSTEAD OF A LIMITED NUMBER OF TIMES. I honestly do not understand how they keep shooting themselves in the foot like this. They try to mush previous games features into the live service mold instead of finding new ways to add to the live service.

- This is an obvious one but I have to mention it. $20 skin pack microtransactions in a full priced $70 game is ridiculous. You aren't getting a single dime out of me. Cosmetics and Battlepasses that cost real money is a monetization method for Free to Play games. This game costs $70 and has more predatory MTX than The Finals which is an entirely Free to Play game. You can't have your cake and eat it too, but somehow AAA studios have found a way.

Despite all that they still added some fantastic things that I can't help but miss when I play older BF games.
- Dragging is a fantastic feature that is pretty much perfectly implemented. Feels great to do and very rarely bugs out.
- The loop from when you die, to being revived is entirely seamless and very immersive. 
- Performance and graphics are overall very good, but not phenomenal.
- The new Escalation gamemode started off rough, but they've made the matches way longer and it's actually really fun and one of the best additions to the game.
- Weapons are very sexy and feel pretty good to use. Weapon customization is pretty solid.
