É muito triste ver como a EA pegou mais uma de suas melhores franquias e enfiou no rabo.

Os melhores BF's de guerra moderna foram o 3 e depois o 4. Daí pra frente foi uma regressão e praticamente um desrespeito aos fãs. 

O tão aguardado BF6 nada mais é do que o BF 2042 que a EA ainda está corrigindo.

Pontos fortes:
- Tem um discord onde dizem que escutam a comunidade.
- Pelo menos a versão paga tem uma campanha.
- É um jogo casual.
- Tem boas opções de personalização de armas.
- Tem um modo battle royale pra quem gosta.

Pontos fracos:
- Gameplay terrivelmente genérico.
- Muitos modos de jogo que não agregam nem mudam o estilo de gameplay.
- Servidores com muitos bots (pois não tem muitas pessoas jogando depois do hype).
- Crossplay do inferno. Pra quem joga no pc, não é possível desativar e obviamente quem é do console tem muitas assistencias. Difícil de balancear isso.
- Aeronaves e veículos medíocres.  Pilotagem de Helis e Jatos terrível (mais um indício de ser o 2042 mascarado).
- Times NATO e PAX Armata muito genéricos e sem expressão. (Infelizmente optaram por não colocar a Russia no game. Lembrando que no BF4 tinham US, Russia e China. Nesse "acharam melhor não falar de guerra").
- Levolution: Cadê? já era! Priorizaram combates de infantaria e pequenas destruições, talvez um a parede de prédio, mas está longe da interação com ambiente que existia no BF4.
- Mapas nada de mais.
- Acabaram as dlcs. Claro que o formato atual visa ser mais lucrativo, mas ter que ficar comprando passe de batalha e moedinhas pra destravar cosméticos é lamentável. Pelo menos são só cosmétivos e não afetam no gameplay.

Writing this review as of the announcement of Season 2.

The game itself is good in terms of its core gameplay, even though many veteran players point out a lot of issues compared to older battlefields. Destruction is the best it has ever been in the series, just without the levolution mechanics seen in BF4, which is a shame, but nevertheless you can destroy way more stuff than in any previous entry of the series and it feels good as well. Graphics are also good, just a bit more bland than for example the visual artstyle of BF1 for its time, but no complaints in this regard.

However, the real and biggest flaw of this game is its direction and future outlook. What started out as a fairly grounded game slowly but steadily turns into a fortnified large scale combat game. Every new skin added into the game is progressively more goofy and in my opinion just looks awful - instead of authentic looking "John Soldier" military skins, we are getting something AI would generate if you asked it for a "Super cool kickass main character soldier". The final result looks something like a dude with a halloween mask, hood over his head, riot gear on his limbs and all that in bright yellow color. Fortnite truly ruined gaming when even military themed games start looking like dress to impress in roblox.
On top of all this - the game gets almost 0 post launch content, despite it having barely any content on launch in the first place. We get 2 new maps in the span of the next 4 months, but at least we can have a battle pass, FOMO limited time modes and AI generated cosmetics.

I want to clarify why it is a bad Battlefield game in my honest opinion;

-TTK is way too fast. Related to that, self healing is waaay too powerful. It should not start so quickly and should not heal so fast.

-Maps are too claustrophobic and there are waaay too many places to hide and camp. I know hiding and camping was always in the BF but in BF6 it is at a ridiculous level.

-I don't think sniper sweet spot mechanic should be in a BF game. Meaning, under no circumstances they should be able to one shot kill a player with full HP. Unless of course, they land a headshot! On a related note maybe they should bring back the old suppression mechanic, which increases your random bullet deviation.

-Seems like vehicle gameplay was an afterthought and most of the maps do not properly accommodate vehicles.

-Tanks should not have guided munitions! It encourages tank drivers to stay back and do not engage in frontline combat. I mean, yeah, in older BFs, some tank drivers were doing exactly that anyways but it is now easier than ever.

-I don't like open weapon systems but I have to admit it is a minor thing compared to what I mentioned above.

Ok, the game genuinely seems fun, and I would probably have more to say on that topic if it ran properly on my computer. I'd like to play it more, and maybe I will in the future if I get a console / dedicated machine for it.

But after getting the game, I later found out it uses kernel level permissions for its anticheat (EA Javelin Anticheat), which is becoming an increasingly more popular practice. I love that Valve requires game that use such permissions to say so on the store page, as it really helps on the topic.

The reason I take issue with this is because its a direct violation of the Principle of Least Privilege (PoLP). Its not core to the functionality of the game. And on principle, a video game isn't nearly important enough the have the same kind of permissions other software has thats core to functionality of the device. It sets bad industry standards, and as a result, user expectations on what kind of permissions other software generally needs.

Its a fun game, and has a lot of really cool mechanics, from what I can see. But this comment is mostly to apply whatever minuscule level of pressure I can vote for better dev practices in the industry.

Users can do what they want with their computer. I'm not one to get in the way of that. But do keep in mind they're also the biggest security risk.

And again, Steam does have this nice little section of the store page that requires sellers to say if their game requires kernel level permissions.

Review Title: 200+ Hours Verdict: Great Combat Ruined by Bugs, Cheaters, and Greed
Overall Verdict: Recommended (7.5/10)
After 217 hours, I can say this game is truly enjoyable in bursts, but there are some atrocious, frustrating issues that cannot be ignored. These flaws make the experience repulsive at times.

The "Ugly" Side (Issues & Bugs):

1-The Insane Weapon Grind: It is hard to understand the logic behind forcing a player to take on an "extra work shift" just to unlock attachments. Requiring over 3,000 kills to unlock all attachments for a single weapon is pure madness. Reaching the max weapon level can take 1,500+ kills, with later levels needing over 44,000+ XP.

2-Game-Breaking Glitches: On Operation Firestorm, snipers are prone and invisible to hits—even when their whole head is visible, shots don't register.

3-Map Exploits: On Iberian Offensive (Objective C), players reach rooftops that should be unreachable. This map is riddled with errors I reported at launch that still aren't fixed.

4-Cheaters & RedSec: The free-to-play RedSec mode has opened the floodgates for cheaters, making Battle Royale unplayable.

5-Broken Physics: Tank and vehicle explosions leave parts floating in the air until the match ends. It looks very poorly optimized and ruins the immersion.

The "Greed" Factor:

Pricing: Paying $60 for the game plus $10 for a Battle Pass is extreme. It’s the price of a full legendary game on sale.

Final Thought:
The core gameplay is fun, but the technical failures, the cheaters, and this ridiculous "work-shift" progression kill the enjoyment. Fix the game and respect our time! 
Aiden

Right now, I cannot recommend the game. It had so much potential to be the best FPS out there, but DICE decided to do otherwise. The game has its moments, but ultimately it underdelivered.

The movement is too much like CoD, with air strafes and mid-air headshots—if they even register. There is a very narrow selection of maps, most of which are small. Vehicles spawn-camp and destroy everything. You want to fly? Not in this game, because base-camping AA will ground you before you even take off.

But the worst part, at least for me, is gun progression. It takes around 1,500 kills with a gun to level it to 50, which unlocks the special version. Some must-have attachments are available only at higher gun levels, so to play comfortably, you have to grind. Boosts help only a little, and with Portal farming nerfed into the ground, they make no sense.

Speaking of Portal—DICE killed it. They may say it’s our fault, but it’s theirs. People leveled guns and did challenges there because doing them in normal gameplay was horrendous and inefficient. But that way, they couldn’t sell enough of their lame boosts, so they nerfed it.

And the battle pass—crème de la crème of grind. At higher levels, you get one tick every few matches. You can do challenges, but if you’re unlucky like I am, you’ll get several Redacted or Gauntlet ones, with only four reroll chances. The best way to fully level the battle pass is to buy tier skips.

If I remember correctly, there were two time-limited events this season. Both sucked hard, in my humble opinion. FOMO exists in this game like nowhere else.

Supposedly, they fixed or changed the aspects I’m mentioning in Season 2. We’ll see—but I don’t have high hopes for this game right now.

And one last note: take what I said with a grain of salt. Your experience might be different than mine, and that’s good. We have different tastes, so if the game appeals to you, kind stranger, have fun!

The game is in a bad state right now. The gunplay feels terrible, weapons are poorly tuned, and ghost bullets are still a thing. You can dump half a mag into someone, only for them to turn around and kill you in five bullets.

The engine doesn’t help either — it feels like the internal FPS is low, like there’s built-in input delay or sluggishness during firefights. It just makes everything feel inconsistent and frustrating.

DayZ stands as one of the most influential and uncompromising survival games ever created. Rather than guiding players with scripted missions or artificial progression systems, it delivers something far more powerful: genuine, unscripted human stories born from tension, scarcity, and survival instinct.

Set in the hauntingly atmospheric post-Soviet landscape of Chernarus, DayZ creates an environment that feels bleak, authentic, and intensely immersive. The massive open world is meticulously crafted, featuring abandoned villages, decaying industrial complexes, dense forests, and coastal towns that all feel eerily real. Exploration is slow, deliberate, and meaningful—every building entered carries risk, every distant gunshot triggers adrenaline.

What makes DayZ exceptional is its emergent gameplay. There are no quest markers or hand-holding mechanics; survival depends entirely on your decisions. Food, water, medical supplies, and ammunition are scarce. Combat is brutal and unforgiving. One mistake can erase hours of progress, which makes every encounter—friendly or hostile—deeply consequential.

The player interaction system is where DayZ truly shines. Every meeting with another survivor becomes a psychological experience. Trust, betrayal, cooperation, and deception all unfold naturally. Some of the most memorable moments in gaming come not from scripted events, but from spontaneous human interactions within this sandbox.

Mechanically, the survival systems are robust and grounded. Players must manage hunger, hydration, temperature, illness, and stamina. The weapon handling feels weighty and realistic, with meaningful recoil and ballistics. The crafting and base-building systems add long-term strategic depth for those who want to establish dominance or create safe havens.

Visually, the atmosphere is outstanding. Dynamic weather, shifting daylight cycles, and haunting environmental audio design create constant tension. The silence of a forest can be just as intense as a firefight in a military base.

Most impressively, DayZ continues to evolve. Ongoing updates, server customization, and an active modding community keep the experience fresh and adaptable. Whether you prefer hardcore vanilla survival or heavily modded roleplay servers, the game accommodates a wide range of playstyles.

In conclusion, DayZ is not just a game—it is a survival simulator that delivers raw, unscripted human drama. Few titles generate this level of tension, immersion, and emotional impact.

Rating: 9.5/10 – A landmark survival experience that remains unmatched in emergent gameplay.

DayZ is one of the most immersive survival games you can play. It doesn’t hold your hand, and that’s exactly what makes it special. Every life feels like its own story — from scrambling to find food and basic gear to tense encounters with other players where you’re never sure if they’ll help you or shoot you.

The atmosphere is where DayZ really shines. The map is huge, quiet, and sometimes eerily peaceful, which makes dangerous moments hit even harder. A simple gunshot in the distance or footsteps in a building can spike your adrenaline instantly. Few games create that level of tension naturally.

The survival mechanics are solid too. Managing hunger, thirst, injuries, and sickness keeps you thinking ahead. It’s not just a shooter — it’s about planning, risk, and patience. Traveling for an hour and finally finding good loot feels genuinely rewarding.

It’s not perfect. It can be slow, and new players might find it punishing. Bugs and jank still pop up sometimes. But if you give it time, the freedom and player-driven stories make it worth it. Playing with friends makes it even better.

A hardcore, immersive survival experience where every life tells a story. One of the best in the genre. 👍

After nearly 300 hours of playing and more than eight years of waiting out patches, I can honestly say this is the one game that never managed to live up to its potential. It had everything going for it, an ambitious concept, years of hype, lots of community goodwill and in the end result it feels like a constant reminder of what could have been rather than what is.

I’ve had moments of genuine fun. There are flashes of brilliance where you can see the core idea shine through, the atmosphere, the scale, and the unique experiences that capture what the developers originally hyped up. But those moments are fleeting, buried under layers of clunkiness, dated mechanics, and technical issues that make the experience far more frustrating than fun.

Even after countless overhyped patches patches, the game is still rough around the edges. Interface bugs, inconsistent performance, and strange design decisions constantly drag things down. What’s worse is that cheating still continues to be a serious, game breaking issue. Hackers are rampant, spawning objects, flying through walls, and generally causing chaos and the developers seem unwilling or unable to get it under control. It completely undermines any sense of fairness or immersion.

After all these years, it’s disappointing to see a project with so much potential still mired in the same problems it’s had from it's early. At this point, it's clear it won't ever reach the standard it once promised and it's evident that Bohemia don't care and can't be trusted to fulfil it's potential

Here’s a detailed review of **Euro Truck Simulator 2 (ETS2)**, blending expert opinions with long-term player experiences:

---

## 🚚 Overview
Euro Truck Simulator 2, developed by **SCS Software**, is a truck-driving simulation game where players transport cargo across a highly detailed map of Europe. Since its release in 2012, it has grown through expansions and mods, becoming one of the most beloved simulation titles worldwide.

---

## Strengths
- **Immersive Driving Experience**  
  The game captures the rhythm of long-haul trucking: engine hums, dashboard glow, and weather effects create a meditative atmosphere. Many players describe it as relaxing rather than stressful.  [visualfoodie.com](https://visualfoodie.com/an-honest-review-of-euro-truck-simulator-2-today/)  

- **Expansive World**  
  ETS2’s map covers much of Europe, with DLCs adding regions like Scandinavia, Italy, and the Iberian Peninsula. The scale and detail make exploration rewarding.  [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vr48P-QzE1E)  

- **Simulation Depth**  
  Beyond driving, players manage a trucking company—buying vehicles, hiring drivers, and expanding operations. This adds a strategic layer to the experience.  [PCGamer](https://www.pcgamer.com/euro-truck-simulator-2-review/)  

- **Community & Mods**  
  A vibrant modding community enhances realism with custom trucks, traffic packs, and even multiplayer servers.

---

## Weaknesses
- **Repetitive Gameplay**  
  Deliveries can feel monotonous over time, especially without DLCs or mods.  [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vr48P-QzE1E)  

- **DLC Dependency**  
  The base game is strong, but much of the expanded content requires paid DLCs. Some players feel this fragments the experience.  [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Vr48P-QzE1E)  

- **Learning Curve**  
  New players may find truck handling clumsy at first, especially with manual transmissions and realistic physics.  [visualfoodie.com](https://visualfoodie.com/an-honest-review-of-euro-truck-simulator-2-today/)  

---

## Verdict
Euro Truck Simulator 2 is more than just a driving game—it’s a **meditative simulation** that appeals to both casual players seeking relaxation and enthusiasts who enjoy logistics and company management. While DLCs are almost essential for the full experience, the base game remains a solid entry point.  

If you enjoy slow-paced, immersive gameplay with a focus on realism and exploration, ETS2 is absolutely worth playing—even in 2026, it remains a **benchmark in simulation gaming**.  [visualfoodie.com](https://visualfoodie.com/an-honest-review-of-euro-truck-simulator-2-today/)

The game has been excellent for years, but the Route Advisor introduced with the 1.58 update is a serious downgrade.

I used to keep the Route Advisor hidden and only toggle it on when I needed it with F3. That control is now gone. Forcing in-game notifications to depend on whether the Route Advisor is visible is a fundamentally bad design decision. Information and UI preference should never be locked together.

Having to pause the game and open a large menu just to check truck or trailer damage is absurd. It breaks immersion, disrupts gameplay flow, and works directly against the idea of a driving simulation.

Additional issues:

The new Route Advisor takes up unnecessary screen space and cannot be truly minimized.

Players are forced to accept visual clutter just to receive basic warnings and information.

Long-time muscle memory and established playstyles were ignored.

No proper toggle or legacy option was provided, despite this being a major UI change.

This feels like a console-style UI decision imposed on PC players who value control and efficiency.

In short, HUD information should be modular, and the Route Advisor should be optional. Tying critical notifications to a single, intrusive UI element is a clear regression, not an improvement.

I thought this game would be complex and overwhelming. It turned out to be one of the most relaxing games I’ve played.

Euro Truck Simulator 2 looks deep and intimidating at first, with all its systems and controls, but in practice it’s a very cozy game. Once you get used to the basics, it becomes incredibly chill and enjoyable.

The mechanics are great and feel natural. Driving, managing deliveries, and planning routes is satisfying instead of stressful. For me, the biggest strength of the game was how relaxing it is. It helped me disconnect from reality and spend time in a different world at my own pace.

Customization is another highlight. Both interior and exterior customization are really well done. I spent a lot of time adjusting my truck, changing details, and making it feel personal. There’s also a great variety of trucks, cargo types, and routes, which keeps things fresh.

Since you choose your routes and how you approach each delivery, the experience feels personal and flexible.

If you’re looking for a cozy game to relax, clear your mind, and enjoy a slow and immersive experience, this is an easy recommendation.

For being a game set in space.....they sure do let you skip a whole lot of it. I really don't understand why they made an extensive ship builder for ships that you basically do nothing with. The only space flight you can do is in small sky boxes orbiting the fake jpeg planets.

Want to land? Loading screen. Want to take off? Loading screen. Want to visit another planet? Loading screen. Want to jump to a different system? Loading screen. In fact, you can pretty much avoid space all together by using fast travel. You can fast travel from the surface of a planet to a location in an entirely different system all without seeing or stepping foot in your ship. 

The nail in the coffin for me was a side quest where you had to recover some items for an NPC from shipyard storage. Theres a yard worker and locked door in between you and what you need. After going through the dialogue, the worker says he will call security if you don't leave. I didn't leave, proceeded past the worker with my stolen key card from the security office, grabbed the items and walked right back out past him all without a hitch. Utterly immersion breaking. There's lots of quests like this that just don't make sense and are lazy. 

Starfield is trying to dress up as a space game and fails, and frankly the remaining elements of the game are no better. The planets suck, the space combat sucks, the Ai sucks, the quests suck, the exploration sucks. 

The game is pretty....but that's about it for me. Go play no mans sky, that's what I'm gonna do.

I bought this for Star Wars Genesis, and prior to installing that mod I figured I would at least give the game a shot to see what all the fuss is about.

I don't have much to add that hasn't already been said. It definitely feels like a Bethesda game, except that there's very little to explore that isn't throwaway procedural content. All the Bethesda jank is still present with the positively ancient game engine they stubbornly continue to use, tons of bugs and glitches that won't ever be officially fixed, and awful balancing with the skills and weapons. This is sadly normal for a Bethsoft game, but the redeeming virtue was a handbuilt world full of interesting places to explore. Take that away and you end up with Starfield.

I'm not going to say it's the worst game ever because it's not and it can be fun to play (some mods are practically essential though), but it's definitely a massive disappointment. There's so many missed opportunities in the game and so little interesting content outside the story missions. I kind of see what Todd Howard was going for, but the game missed the mark pretty badly. There's not really an easy fix, what this game needed was a lot more direction and time to flesh things out and there's not much for modders to really work with to properly fix the base game.

If I had to pick some feasible (i.e. not needing to build a completely new engine/game from scratch but still probably a lot of work) things to do to fix the game, here's what I would do:
- Add a LOT more points of interest that can be found (hundreds, see Empyrion Galactic Survival) with multiple variations (different factions/state of repair for a standard outpost layout for example)
- Give earth it's own unique POIs and biomes to actually look like an abandoned planet with the ruins of civilization and have a whole scavenger faction/questline that searches for hidden treasures in the ruins
- Add a lot more hand built locations to make the systems actually feel lived in
- Vastly increase ship cargo hold capacity, especially in the early game
- Rebalance skills to make everything useful in some way even in the end game
- Rebalance resource and crafting, especially weight (crafting magically creates mass out of thin air in way too many recipes)
- Bring back something like VATS, this is a RPG and it was really nice in Fallout to be able to RP a super sniper/gunslinger without personally having the crazy shooting skills
- Rebalance combat so all guns are viable in the end game and have appropriate variants (bonus points for a full combat system overhaul with more realistic gunplay and not the magic damage increases from skill points and pitifully low damage per bullet with full auto, make most guns select fire and make skills affect accuracy, recoil mitigation, reload speed, aim speed, etc, and have weapon damage be calculated primarily from the ammo plus use the barrel length as a lesser modifier).
- Add mechs and small aircraft that can be used on planets

Just like the general vibe of the average reviewer, I have mixed feelings about my experience playing this game.

Overall I find it to be satisfying and engaging. I have certainly gotten many hours of gameplay out of it and that's a difficult bar to clear for any game these days. I enjoy the story, the characters and voice acting even if some of it does seem like generic filler (hey, it's a big game with lots of content). There are a good variety of things to do to keep me busy with like questing, combat, character building, base building, ship building, storytelling etc. You can get sucked into any one of these things and waste endless hours of your life before even noticing, which is what games are for, however...I completely understand why people complain endlessly about it.

Personally, my biggest gripe is the perplexing absence of quality of life features. Things as simple as having a scroll bar enlarge when you hover over it so that you can ACTUALLY target it to move it up and down the screen. I don't know how many times I have made a proper fool of myself trying to click a scroll bar in the inventory just to have it not activate because it's tiny and doesn't automatically enlarge when hovering over it with the cursor. Most primitive websites have figured this out in the 90s yet BS didn't find it prudent to include as a feature. Also, every time you fast travel with a companion following you, they spawn directly in front of you so that you always have to run around them to go in the direction you're intentionally travelling. Did they not play their own game? Did they not have time to fix this obvious persistently annoying issue? Are they purposefully antagonizing me? It boggles the mind. These are just a few of the dozens of amateur-rank QoL features overlooked which makes you wonder how much pressure is put on the devs to wrap up their slice of the pie, and how little regard is allocated to fixing these issues post-launch. 

I also loathe Bethesda's approach to carryweight, inventory management and a cruel penchant for cluttering up the game with completely useless items that can be picked up for no discernable reason. I feel like I'm being mocked by every junk item laying on the ground. It completely takes me out of the game when I have to stop and look up every item to see if it has any use at all, especially when you taunt me with your ridiculous inventory management system. I suppose I'll never have to worry about Alzheimer's trying to memorize all that crap, but that should be my choice, not yours.

Once you figure out how to get around all that annoying rubbish, it can be a pretty fun game worth many hours of play, especially if you like sci fi and spacefaring.

tl;dr: Great open world third-person shooter, horrendous Mass Effect game.

This is another one of those games where I wish Steam had a "Neutral" option. To preface, I played Andromeda immediately after finishing my first playthrough of the Mass Effect series (Legendary Edition), so this review is coming from someone that can be considered "relatively new" to the series.

That being said, if you're expecting a continuation of the main Mass Effect trilogy in Andromeda, you might want to reconsider playing Andromeda. It is WILDLY apparent that Andromeda was made by a different team compared to the OG Mass Effect trilogy. The best way I can describe it is "Walmart Mass Effect". Pretty much the only thing Andromeda has in common with its predecessor are the aliens, and even then, the aliens are cheap knockoff versions of the originals. The Asari ALL have the same face, the Turians are all pale as hell for some reason and look like they're constantly trying to sit in a chair, and the Salarians all look like they're wearing cheap lipstick. It's very uncanny. The story also has almost no ties to the original trilogy except from a few passing comments here and there during side quests that are easily missable. You will not be seeing Shepard or any other characters from the original trilogy, and the closest thing you will get to a cameo are some audio recordings from Liara. Even the villains of Andromeda are just Walmart versions of Mass Effect 2's Collectors - oh no, evil space aliens want to abduct people and steal their DNA! Now where have I seen that before?

However, if you go into Andromeda without any of these expectations, then you're probably going to have a good time. The combat is undeniably the best in the entire franchise. You can literally become a space ninja dashing around and teleporting everywhere with the right build. There is no rigid "class" system, so you can build your character however you like with whatever skills and traits you like - they're really generous with skill points, so don't worry about running out. You can also respec anytime on your ship if you feel like your build is getting stale or underperforming. The closest comparisons I can draw are Warframe and Borderlands, so if you enjoy those games, you'll probably enjoy Andromeda.

The second thing Andromeda does right is exploration. Andromeda really nails the feeling of being "strangers in an entirely new galaxy". Map completion and making worlds habitable by completing quests and tasks is very satisfying. Speaking of quests, there are A LOT of quests. You will probably be overwhelmed the first time you play because Andromeda has a bad habit of just immediately dumping 15-20 side quests on you whenever you land on a new planet. Some side quests are also hidden behind ambient NPC dialogue or just talking to NPCs, so if you're a completionist you might find yourself worrying about whether or not you missed something (don't worry, you WILL miss stuff just because of the sheer amount of content). This is not inherently a bad thing because it just means more content, but some people might find this offputting.

Now onto the objective negatives. The game is buggy as hell. You WILL get stuck in terrain and have to reload saves. Enemies WILL spawn inside walls or out of bounds, making you unable to complete quests where you have to kill every enemy. If you don't stop what you are doing and take your hands off the keyboard/controller whenever someone starts talking (and they talk A LOT), you risk interrupting the dialogue. Sometimes it doesn't even matter - NPCs will walk into you and interrupt dialogue even if you're standing still. SAM (the AI in your head) is infuriating and will NOT SHUT UP. This is especially bad on planets with environmental hazards such as cold or heat. Expect a nonstop barrage of "LIFE SUPPORT IS FAILING" "TEMPERATURE IS DROPPING" "LIFE SUPPORT IS IN RANGE" "TEMPERATURE IS RISING" from SAM every 3 seconds on those planets. And yes, SAM can ALSO interrupt dialogue. Entering and leaving planets also prompts a 30 second unskippable cutscene for some reason (and you're going to be doing that A LOT).

Luckily, there are certain mods that rectify the issues I mentioned, and yes, they're pretty much mandatory in order to make the game playable (in my opinion). MEA Bugfixes, Shut Up SAM, Faster Mining, and Shorter Landing and Departure Cinematics are the ones I absolutely recommend installing before playing. 

All in all, you can have quite a bit of fun with Mass Effect: Andromeda if you completely ignore the fact that they were trying (and failed) to be a Mass Effect game. Just pretend it's like open world Warframe, install the requisite mods, laugh at how bad the Asari and Turian models are, and you'll probably have a great time. 6/10.

Mass Effect Andromeda was a fun foray into the Sci-fi Open World RPG genre. It has a nice little mix of everything, from third person shooter combat, to very basic space exploration, to exploring strange planets. However, reader beware, this is NOT like the Mass Effect Trilogy. There are a lot of similarities, and mechanics that are identical, and a lot that this game took from the trilogy and changed. However, because this game took the open world approach, the story telling is not as linear. It's padded with tons of extra side missions, and tasks (which are basically side side missions). It's to the point where it becomes too much, as most are fetch quests having you running from point a to b, sometimes planet to planet, with nothing more than some minor dialogue (aka no real world building). This isn't too much a of a problem as a lot can be  ignored (Specifically anything labeled "task". Still, it can be overwhelming. 

Overall, the game was still very much enjoyable, and a little sad that there is not and potentially will not be a sequel, but aside from the lingering questions, the main thing that really felt disjointed to me, was the lack of control over squad mates. As the main character you can spec yourself out to play any role from the previous games, and mix it up. Your squadmates, tend to be quite similar in functionality, but you can no longer command them to use their special abilities. It is up the AI to use them, and frankly, the squadmates AI is really rather poor. If you play on Insanity, they practically commit suicide.

That aside, gameplay wise I have no major complaints. It wasn't as smooth as say Mass Effect 3, but it wasn't quite poor either. I don't think it's worth the full price, personally, but I got it on sale for under $10. If you like Mass Effect, like open world games, and like third person shooters, then this is a great game to sink 40-50 hrs (for full achievements, closer to 65-70 hrs).

reviews.review:
I had fun with this game. When I write a description, it just ends up sounding 'pretty good,' but much of the time, I found myself grinning, and more importantly, engaged.

I think that, first, the story and characters are good. Not Andor good, but pretty dank farrik good. The end is a bit rushed, but other than that, I found myself liking the characters, especially Kay and ND-5. Remember how the Clone Wars TV show made you care about clone troopers? Well this game makes you care about a battle droid. It helps that, except for some minor parts, the characters are new, so they have room to develop in the Star Wars galaxy. The main character can have an arc that doesn't have to end with her being a hermit on Tatooine or a smuggler with a debt to Jabba at the end of the story. She and the rest of the characters (who live) can develop without later media constraining their character arcs.

Now, I only recently got and played the game. The gameplay isn't perfect, but in the state its in, it kinda reminds me of Uncharted. From what I've read, when the game first came out, the gameplay was pretty awful. Well, the devs actually stuck with the game, and brought it to a place where it is pretty good action-adventure level. It's pretty good - nothing to write home about, but it also is still fun.

For anyone who is worried about Ubisoft open worlds, I actually found this one to be good. There are no radio towers to climb - you discover locations either by getting really close to them, through quests, or by looking through your binoculars. And while many don't contain loot, they do contain upgrade materials (don't worry, there isn't a crafting system, and if you want, you can buy most materials from merchants anyway), and usually some fun lore. And because of this, I didn't feel the need to 100% the game, and it was better for it. If I visited a location, it was because I wanted to be there for story/quest reasons, or to find some item I learned naturally, or just because the location looked interesting, not because I climbed a tower that revealed a busywork icons on the map.

If it sounds like this isn't the most overwhelming praise, it is because it isn't. Taken individually, all the elements (except for the story, which I actually found pretty dang good) are good, but not great. Despite that, I think the game is more than the sum of its parts. I can't quite describe it, except to say that I had way more fun with this game than I expected, and than it had any right to be, just looking back over my own comments.

TL;DR, this is a good game that is better than the sum of its parts, and I had a lot of fun with it. Definitely worth getting on sale, and maybe full-price if you like open-world games, now that the devs fixed the gameplay and added some free DLC.

TLDR: if you're a Star Wars fan that isn't triggered by playing as a female, and you're also not sick of the 'Ubisoft Open-World Game Design Formulaᵀᴹ', you will have a good time with Star Wars Outlaws.


Pros:
- Beautiful, detailed open-world planets to explore, each one conveys the Star Wars aesthetic wonderfully. The first planet (Toshara) is sci-fi African plains, then there's a smaller city map (Kijimi) set on a cold/snowy planet, Akiva is another (rain-forest themed, this time) large map with explorable settlements throughout, and finally we get what is easily the most believable video game rendition of Tatooine yet (it's huge, Mos Eisley is present and fully explorable). Toshara and Tatooine especially felt like real places to me, they're so well done.

- Loyalty system across four Syndicate factions: pick/choose certain jobs as to not upset the wrong people. 

- Space exploration around the orbit of each planet (Tatooine is explorable, but there's basically nothing there of note). Toshara, Kijimi and Akiva have unique space environments to explore (ship graveyard / Nebula / Asteroid Belt). 

- Strong visuals taking advantage of forward-looking Ray Tracing tech... though there are some caveats to this (see cons list). Excellent art design.

- Cute critter companion. Engaging (if unoriginal) story.

- They absolutely nailed the 'cantina sleaze' vibe they were going for (it's a small thing but I love how you can just lean against the bar and soak in the atmosphere of the various cantinas). The game has a bunch of varied environments, characters and references that fans of this franchise will get a kick out of.

- Lock-picking is a little rhythm mini-game and it took longer than normal for me to get bored of doing it.

- The Speeder is fun and makes open world exploration less tedious (some of these maps are huge). 

- Sabbac (in-universe card game) is awesome once you get the hang of it.

- Personally I like the main character design a lot. There are a bunch of cosmetic options for your character/critter/ship/speeder, too. If playing as a female is such a burden, go play the recent Jedi games (both of which are great imo).

- Command your sci-fi axalotl critter companion to attack/distract enemies, open doors, interact with items etc. I love Nix!

- The HDR implementation is good, lights and engine exhausts look suitably bright/hot. 


Meh:
- Most of the game design is ripped straight out of Ubisoft's basic formula with some Star Wars flavoured tweaks stapled on. Personally I haven't played that many Ubisoft games in recent years, but I imagine if you play every entry of Assassin's Creed or Far Cry you will find most everything here boring or familiar (especially if you're not a Star Wars fan... but if you're not a fan, honestly why are you even bothering with this game?). That said there are a few unique features that fit the theme/setting well, for example: trying to talk out of getting caught when in stealth, and cheating at Sabbac in various ways. For the most part it's competently designed, but there's very little 'new' here.

- Sometimes you get caught in stealth when it doesn't feel like you should. Other times you wonder how these NPCs didn't notice you wolf whistle and upper cut their buddy who is standing right next to them (for the most part the stealth is functional though).

- Kay has all the usual 'Video Game Protagonistᵀᴹ' abilities: press button to scan environment for interactables, grapple rope to climb/swing, ability to climb certain walls or yellow painted railings etc. If you've played Tomb Raider or Uncharted you've experienced all of this before. Certain routes or collectibles are locked behind Metroidvania style 'ability gates' (rock barriers only destroyable with a specific blaster upgrade etc) but the game is decent enough to mark these on the map if you don't have the required tool yet. One of these skills (a cutting tool that lets you pass certain metal fences) isn't awarded until very near the end of the game; I take issue with this kind of design when it's paced this poorly, as by the time you're granted the ability you're either sick of playing (or the game is effectively over). 

- Further to the above, personally I didn't find the space combat that engaging as too many essential abilities (dodge rolling etc) are - again - locked behind upgrade quests, and by the time these functions were unlockable I'd already explored/completed the space content. Without these upgrades the ship combat felt too simple/boring.

- Maybe I have dementia but certain things aren't explained well in-game and I had to use Google to find out what the fuck I was doing wrong. I didn't understand how to play Sabbac at all during the tutorial (I swear it doesn't tell you the matching cards have to be different colours!) and I didn't realise you could extend/shorten your grappling rope until I was two thirds of the way through the game (there are an on-screen prompts for this at specific grappling points, I just didn't notice it).

- Given the 'outlaws' theme of this game it would've benefitted from more 'morally grey' quests with difficult choices or 'unwinnaable' outcomes (where there is no 100% positive solution) ala Phantom Liberty from Cyberpunk 2077.


Cons:
- This is probably the buggiest game I've ever played on PC in terms of stability. I've honestly lost count of the amount of times the game crashed, though I will say it was mostly from reloading saves or fast travelling... I don't think the game likes certain save states, which is probably why it doesn't let you manually save inside certain areas (that otherwise create autosaves). Also, you'll notice downed enemies respawn when you have to reload saves within these areas, it's like the programming is unable to account for NPCs that aren't in a default state. The save states in this game are kinda dogshit and I ended up forcing myself to manually save every now and then to not lose progress. I don't think my rig is the issue (Ryzen 5900x, 32GB RAM, RTX 5080) as you'll notice the Steam discussion board is rife with players moaning about crashes.

- Ray Tracing and DLSS are awesome technologies but they come with caveats and their limitations are more noticeable here than in anything else I've played. There is noticeable instability in the lighting/shadows (which often have an unattractive swimming/warbling appearance) and I also found that certain effects were either bugged (for example the heat haze effects on radiators/cooking equipment, check it out when you reach the top of the stairs upon leaving the cantina on Kijimi) or sometimes outright missing (some laser effects, blaster fire, sparks etc) as they were probably lost in the temporal mush this tech relies on. It's possible something isn't right with the way this tech is implemented, which is a shame because the game can often look absolutely stunning. This was all noted at max settings!

- Some animations lack weight, just seem generally goofy/robotic, or in the worst cases are bugged. The first time you sneak behind a Storm Trooper and watch Kay knock-out a fully armoured man bare-handed you'll probably laugh! I wondered why they didn't just give her a taser initially, but it turns out that's an unlockable ability that enables you to KO elite enemies and droids. Fair enough - but why couldn't she have started off with a baton or something to make this less silly (bare-knuckled KOs against unarmoured enemies look fine imo). Climbing in general feels poor in this game as sometimes prompts don't appear (causing Kay to awkwardly rub against a wall instead of grabbing it) or the character jumps off in a random direction. Lip sync during cutscenes is not great, and lighting can flash or freak out during camera cuts.



Still reading? Overall: I really enjoyed my time with this game despite its faults, and would recommend it to Star Wars fans

Like a Star Wars theme park ride? It nails the look and feel in great detail and it tries to give you a taste of excitement. Except for an occasional thrill, it never feels like there are real consequences to your actions..
I indulged in side questing and exploration. Once you get off your speeder fat bike most of the game involves platforming and solving puzzles with switches. I can sneak like a thief, but the weapon upgrades are OP and after some time you shrug off blaster fire like a Twi'lek dancer does her cloves.

After spending around 26 hours with the game I can’t say I enjoyed the experience.

I really disliked the core gameplay mechanics and the main character’s movement and physics. Combat, shooting and general character control feel very repetitive and low quality, with almost the same animations and actions used over and over again. Nothing felt fresh or innovative.

The world feels empty and lifeless. I had no real motivation to explore the environment or complete side quests, as everything felt dull and unengaging. Mission design relies heavily on puzzles and there are simply too many of them. They quickly become tedious, boring, and exhausting, to the point where I just wanted everything to end as soon as possible.

The graphics are good, and performance/stability is relatively okay, which are the game’s main positives. However, the story was not interesting for me at all. I would rate it 5 out of 10. The missions were so uninteresting that I rushed through the story just to see the ending.

Overall, despite decent visuals and acceptable performance the repetitive gameplay, lifeless world and boring mission structure made this a disappointing experience for me...

I’m honestly disappointed :((((  especially considering the price I paid for this game. In my opinion it is absolutely not worth the asking price and does not justify its cost in terms of content, quality, or overall enjoyment.
Crashing often usung RTX Direct Lighting with 5070. Sometimes crashing without it. But game is okay mostly, like story and gameplay. With FG and DLSS i have my 160 fps. So it more Yes, then No.

Really loving this game. Just a good story from beginning to end, no play to win, and doesn't feel like a second job! Very refreshing amongst other modern IPs - just sit down, play and enjoy the Star Wars emersion.

Had some issues with the graphical quality being inconsistent, sometimes looked great and sometimes like playdough people, but that could be my system and was mainly resolved by running in windowed mode. Other than that really fun game, felt immersive and has a lot to like.

[b]Think twice[/b] before you buy this, even on a significant discount. This game had(s) a lot of potential to fill a legitmate Star Wars RPG void that nobody has attempted, and despite all the carbonite(lol) copies they could have picked from, they chose to reinvent the wheel. This is your typical Ubisoft slop with a Star Wars skin and a very mild attempt - from both companies - at staying relevant.

Yes, it's a good game, although far from a 9/10, which is what the setting, the name, and Ubisoft's generally positive track record with major titles might have suggested. It's beautiful, creates a unique atmosphere (ultimately through audio and visuals), and when it does feel "realistic," it actually is. I got it on sale.

It's basically Assassin's Creed on alien planets, which is fun in itself if you're into that sort of thing. It works quite well, is more stealth than blunt combat, and as others have already noted, the protagonist has a punch that puts even Mike Tyson and Bud Spencer to shame. In that sense, the gameplay isn't anything new, has hardly any flaws, and offers the familiar range of actions. Since Force powers play almost no role here, these actions are more physical in nature and therefore limited.

Technically, it's okay; it rarely crashes, and sometimes the character or bike gets stuck in some glitch, but you're usually safe thanks to constant saving (automatic or manual). This surprises me, because that never happened in AC Odyssey, for example, and you realize that SWO's technology must come from the same corner as soon as you whistle for the scooter... 🤦‍♂️

The major drawback, in my opinion, is the story and the character herself. You need a considerable amount of "suspension of disbelief" to really get into the story. First of all, there simply doesn't seem to exist a compelling reason why Kay Wess is doing what she's doing – like in other Star Wars stories where you have to save the galaxy or fight the Templars in AC. It seems to me that she just takes her pet Nix out of boredom and decides to become a galaxy-wide wanted gangster instead of a local pickpocket. That Nix doesn't have a care tag is surprising to me anyway, but that's Disney for you…

Furthermore, it's just as “logical” that every criminal organization was simply waiting for someone to come along and carry out their orders as it is that the empire, despite its massive presence, is clueless as always.

You wouldn't guess that Kay is supposedly a young woman in her early to mid-twenties (?) from her looks, and due to a lack of continuity (the movie term), some of her dialogue and behavior come across like that of an inexperienced 20-year-old, while others resemble those of an older, hardened gangster, even though they occur consecutively within the same mission. It's just odd. Kay “always" introduces herself to NPCs seemingly and without being asked, but only when it would make sense in the dialogue or the story does she omit it – to give just one striking example. 

Besides and as the one red line through the complete Star Wars universe, most of the interactions happen in and at bars. That's neat somehow but completely unrealistic, as a crowd in a bar would make a perfect place for any cop to observe suspects, as is known from basically any criminal TV series, novel or documentary. 

Conclusion after 17 hours of relaxed gameplay: An opulent work that scores points for me with its AC gameplay, beautiful "stage design" and fitting sound, but loses massively due to the superficiality of the staging, the dialogue direction and the "script" in general, besides smaller technical problems.

It's a fun game with good stealth aspects, the story is fun, but hasn't fully drawn me in yet. I bought this game on sale, and I think I'd be disappointed if I payed full price. Some parts of the game feel rough or unrefined, while others are done well enough to feel new. Overall 6.8/10

This is a fantastic demonstration of an understaniding of the atmosphere of certain locations in the Star Wars IP. It feels really cool to explore the environments in this game. It feels very "lived-in" for lack of a better phrase. That being said, every time Kay Vess says "Dank farrik," it makes me want to behave unkindly. The writing really is some grade-A horse hockey in this video game. It has the tone of that episode of The Mandalorian with Jack Black and Lizzo and Doc Brown are there and Baby Yoda helps Lizzo with her ball game. Also the little creature that follows you around is transparently the dragon from How To Train Your Dragon but with 6 ears. the melee animations are crazy in this game.

If you can ignore all that though, it's a really cool experience. I'd recommend it on the basis of "it's cool to explore these environments if you like Star Wars."

Review's thumbs-down based on my preferences not the game's quality. The game is good if you are into the genre, but for me it has too many elements and mechanics that don't interest me - I abandoned the playthrough specifically when I got to the level where I'm informed that there are three competing factions and I have to manage my alliances and reputations with each. A letdown after having greatly enjoyed all the Jedi games. But again, that's a "doesn't work for me" problem.

Also too many boring cut-scenes without the benefit of telling a story that made me even remotely engaged. If he storytelling was strong I would put difficulty on Easy mode and plow ahead, but also it's an open, large game and I'm not sitting through 30h+ for a basic playthrough (it's way more if you chase completionist goals).

It's a pity because the Star Wars content is excellent, even if not super creative (i.e. protagonist has mandatory cute sidekick just like Cal Kestis has BD-1) and as a more open world game you really feel living in that universe. And I'm a huge SW fan, still, the gameplay has to work.

I am enjoying the game and will keep playing it. Sadly, I cannot recommend it to the average gamer. To enjoy this game as I do, you both need to be very tolerant of woefully unfinished games, and also a particular love for the genre of stealth action games with RPG mechanics. It's a gorgeous game, with lots of rich locations and quests to immerse you in the Star Wars world. Unfortunately, it's plagued with issues.

I have up to date drivers and crash 2-3 times per session. This is maybe 2 times per hour, as I don't play long sessions. The loading times are incredibly inconsistent. Sometimes, you can die and repeat the same level that just loaded reasonably fast 5 times in a row, and hit one that takes much much longer. I regularly walk and find that the geometry has not yet loaded in the area I'm visiting, and I can walk under the floor because I went faster than the game. I have very fast computer. And the difficulty scaling is all over the place. Playing on default difficulty settings varies from extremely easy to extremely challenging and frustrating, depending on the mission and how poorly they've scripted it. In particular the missions "Partners" and "False Flag" were extremely frustrating for me.

[url=https://www.ubisoft.com/help/connectivity-and-performance/article/reinstalling-supporting-software/000062655]Reinstall supporting software[/url] such as DirectX and the Visual C++ 2015 to 2022 Redistributable.
Reinstall [url=https://dotnet.microsoft.com/download/dotnet-framework] .NET Framework [/url] using the newest version available.

[url=https://help.steampowered.com/faqs/view/6AD7-820D-8BE5-E51F#:~:text=From%20your%20Steam%20Client%2C%20open,Cache%22%20button%20at%20the%20bottom]Clear Steam Cache folder[/url]

Personally, I really enjoyed this game; it's much better now than it was at launch. As much as I like stealth builds, being a big The Last of Us fan, it was good now to be able to blast your way out of situations instead of failing missions.
​The graphics are awesome and I had no performance issues. I averaged around 180fps, reaching up to 240fps in space—that is using a 9800X3D and a 9070 XT, using FSR4 on Quality with Max Ultra settings.
​The only downside was when I tried to complete the game 100%. I like to finish games I enjoy to 100% because, most of the time, you find missions, gear, etc., that you would never come across playing the game linearly. However, two of the trophies, especially one space trophy, were so frustrating I almost quit trying to fully complete the game. Apart from that, it's a great game; the visuals and the atmosphere are the best I've seen in any Star Wars game.

Fun game

If you're into Cyberpunk and are looking for the vibe of playing a character in the criminal underworld, working for crime syndicates reputation and taking jobs from middle men that cyberpunk would call them "Fixers" and here they're called "Brokers" this game is for you.
A great and fun game set in the criminal underworld and you're working your way up with each of the crime syndicates of the Galaxy

[h1] This shouldn't have worked so well! [/h1]

[h2]TLDR:[/h2] The game combines elements from Shadow of the Tomb Raider, The Witcher 3 and Freelancer into a fun adventure that can easily entertain you for 30+ hours. If that sounds good to you, don't listen to the haters and give it a try.

I think this game just got too much hate for all the bugs upon release, the mismanaged marketing and because it's just cool to hate on both Star Wars and Ubisoft nowadays. Of course the game has flaws. I’d even say none of what it does is perfect by itself, but in combination you’ll get a unique experience that’s so much more than the sum of its parts.

[h2]Here's what you'll probably enjoy:[/h2]
[list]
[*] The gameplay mechanics are very solid when it comes to shooting, stealth and exploring. It feels like 90% Shadow of the Tomb Raider which I'd consider the perfect execution.
[*] Interacting with the environment through your pet Nix is unique and allows for many good moments in exploration and combat.
[*] The world is beautifully handcrafted and full of details. None of the procedurally generated slob you find in many open world games nowadays.
[*] The ability system is well implemented and organically grows with your playstyle. It doesn’t feel like an arbitrary skill tree built around artificial XP points.
[*] The gameplay variety is immense and the pacing serves it well. You’ll never have to fight, sneak, riddle or explore too much at once.
[*] The world and quest design remind me a lot of The Witcher 3 with all the things you can do on the side. This goes on beyond the main story and can easily double your playtime if you enjoy the ride. I probably put 10+ hours in just playing Sabacc and upping my game with better shift tokens and cheating abilities. There are also environmental riddles, speeder races and arcade machines if you need a break from the adventure.
[*] The spaceship action takes me back to good old Freelancer days, an itch that only Everspace 2 and Chorus have managed to scratch ever since.
[*] You have plenty options to fine tune difficulty, convenience and HUD settings (with one exception mentioned below).
[/list]

[h2]This you might not like:[/h2]
[list]
[*] The quippy Marvel-like humor rarely lands and you need to just roll with it. It messes with the otherwise great story and characters.
[*] The big syndicate reputation system that Ubisoft marketing focused so heavily on is a joke and wasted potential. There are no lasting consequences for your choices and the cartels don’t really interact with each other. I’d recommend just staying on “good” terms with every syndicate (which you can even buy with data cards) and ignoring it for the rest of the game.
[*] Progression mostly comes through your abilities, tools and upgrading ship and speeder. Outfits and charms don’t do much and in the end there are only 2 or 3 outfits that make sense anyway (fortunately there’s transmog to get something out of the many clothes).
[*]The riddles are quite easy and generally revolve around observing the environment. Only the secret Jet Kordo questline is a tougher nut to crack.
[*] Speeder controls are very direct and not fun in my opinion.
[*] Climbing controls are weird and feel a bit clunky with the subpar camera.
[*] Despite the many settings, you can’t disable the button prompt for mounting objects and climbing walls which is just dumb and immersion breaking. There are mods to disable this, but why is it even there in the first place?
[*] Judging by other reviews there are performance and optimization issues. I played via Geforce Now Ultimate and it crashed only twice in over 70+ hours. However, one of these crashes put me back 3 hours as the autosave didn't synchronize. So if you play via GFN, make sure to manually save every once in a while.
[/list]

For me, the good parts far outweigh the annoyances and I’m glad I gave it a try. General advice for every (non-service) game: Wait until it’s fully patched and all DLCs are released, then only check current “after the hype” or “x years later” reviews. You might regret skipping this gem now that it’s complete.

From what I saw before I got sick of the constant crashes, it's a lot like a stealth version of Jedi: Fallen Order.  If you liked that, this is almost as good...if you can get it to run for more than 20 minutes at a time.  I'd suggest trying the demo first.

reviews.review: Buy at a discount, its alright, victim of the complete capitalisation of games, you get the sense the devs had more to put in this game but it was cut down to fit other agendas.
great game
Good game, enjoyable.

A good depth to the game, in very familiar settings (but why do we always have to go back to Tatooine? The farthest point away from the bright center of the galaxy... c'mon, there's gotta be better places to go!)
The main character, Kay Vess, tends to script out as just a little *too* inexperienced, unfortunately. If she's supposedly some street kid with a bit of a background in being a scoundrel, she should probably have a bit better dialog than "oh, uh... sure!" She might be in over her head, but not tipping her cards at every interaction should be second nature to her, or getting duped into every bad situation. A good character visual design, however, as it's obvious that she's had her nose broken at least once. That kind of storytelling detail is always a mark of passion for the art in my opinion.
Gameplay is good; albeit not unfamiliar to those of us who have played SW: Jedi Survivor and such. Sometimes the "obvious target" for a switch or lever isn't very obvious at all, but that happens, especially during a firefight. Expect to suffer a few deaths until you wind up seeing the solution on some things. Some of the gameplay feels much like the movie "Last Man Standing" (with Bruce Willis) where you're committed to playing one group of gangsters against the other. Voice acting is good, the little cameos here and there sets the time period for the events (if that makes a difference for you), and overall it's a fun game.
90 min into the game with 3 crashes. This is ridiculous.

reviews.review: MAKE SHER YOU HAVE 10 OR MORE GB OF VRAM YOU WILL HAVE A BAD TIME PLAYING IF YOU DONT

Star Wars Outlaws is Ubisoft and Massive Entertainment’s first major open-world Star Wars action-adventure, and it largely succeeds at delivering a vast, lived-in galaxy that feels both familiar and fresh for longtime fans. You play as the scoundrel Kay Vess, a non-Force-using protagonist whose journey across richly varied planets like Tatooine, Akiva, Kijimi, and Toshara mixes shooting, stealth, space travel, and exploration, all underpinned by a dynamic reputation system that affects how different criminal syndicates treat you. The world is dense with activities — from side missions and expert challenges to hull-down bounties and planet-spanning exploration — giving real freedom beyond the linear corridors typical of previous Star Wars action games.

Visually and thematically, Outlaws captures the spirit of the Star Wars universe with authentic environments, bustling cities, and cinematic setpieces that evoke the feel of living in a galaxy “far, far away.” However, unlike titles such as Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order or Star Wars Jedi: Survivor, which unfold as guided, narrative-driven adventures with predetermined levels and pacing, Outlaws’ open world offers freeform play — letting you roam, engage in side content, and tackle objectives in many orders and styles. This gives it a scale and sense of discovery that Jedi games hint at but never fully embrace, even though the pacing and combat can at times feel less refined or punchy compared to those more focused titles.

That open structure will delight players who want the Star Wars sandbox experience with speeder bikes, orbital travel, and branching choices, though it can also highlight some of the game’s flaws: repetitive mission design, occasional technical hitches, and stealth or traversal systems that don’t always live up to their potential. Still, for anyone yearning for something closer to a Star Wars world you can live in rather than just play through, Star Wars Outlaws represents a substantial and generally rewarding evolution of the franchise’s gameplay.

reviews.review:
I recommend the game if you can't wait until the sequel of Jedi Survivor to return exploring Star Wars Galaxy and accept that you must abandon the use of Force. 
General feeling is that it's a less polished Jedi Survivor without Force powers (at least one location in both games seems exactly the same). Force is used only once in the whole game and people witnessing it are as freaked out as people from our own world would be.
The hero of the game has Galaxy's worst haircut (which you can't customize) and so little character that she is left in shadows by her own sidekicks. But I found while playing that it doesn't much disturb me - the main character of the story is perhaps the Star Wars Galaxy itself. 
Still, something is constantly happening to you and your crew and its never not cool seeing three moons rising over a desert night or jumping to hyperspace in your personal starship.
